འདི་ལྟར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དག་པ་ཞེས་པས་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཤེས་བྱའི་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་དབར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་ཡེ་ནས་གཟུང་བ་དང་འཛིན་པ་ཀུན་ཉོན་དང་རྣམ་བྱང་བདག་དང་གཞན་དངོས་དང་དངོས་མེད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གཉིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་གང་དུའང་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་ཐིག་ལེ་ཉག་གཅིག་གདོད་ནས་སྐྱེ་འགག་དང་བྲལ་བའི་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་རང་བཞིན་རྣམ་དག་སྒྲིབ་བྲལ་ཆེན་པོར་གནས་སུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་། དེ་ལྟར་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་འཁྲུལ་པ་གློ་བུར་བ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚེ་ན་བདག་དང་ཆོས་སུ་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་པའི་བློ་དྲི་མ་ཅན་གྱི་ངོར་ཡུལ་ཡང་མ་དག་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་ལ་བློས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་བཟུང་བས་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་དྲི་མ་དང་སྒྲིབ་པ་ཡོད་པ་ལ་མ་དག་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གློ་བུར་གྱི་དྲི་མ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཐེག་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་ལམ་བསྟན་པ་དེ་ལ་ཞུགས་པས་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གནས་ལུགས་རང་བཞིན་རྣམ་དག་དེ་ཇེ་གསལ་དུ་མཐོང་བའི་ཚུལ་ལས་འདི་ལྟར་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དང་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་མཐོང་ལམ་དང་སྒོམ་ལམ་ས་དགུའི་རྟོགས་པ་སྐྱེས་ཏེ་སྤང་བྱའི་དྲི་མ་རྣམས་སྤང་བའི་ཆ་ནས་དག་པ་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་སུ་བརྗོད་དེ་དེ་དག་ནི་དྲི་མ་ཅི་རིགས་པར་དག་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ལ་ཡེ་ནས་མ་དག་པ་མེད་ཀྱང་། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་བཟུང་བའི་དྲི་མ་གློ་བུར་བ་རྣམས་དག་པའི་རིམ་པ་དང་མཚུངས་པས་མིག་སྐྱོན་དག་པས་ཡུལ་ཇེ་གསལ་དུ་མཐོང་བ་ལྟར་ཡུལ་ཅན་དེས་ཡུལ་གྱི་དག་པ་མཐོང་ལ་དེ་མཐོང་བའི་དབང་གིས་ཡུལ་ཅན་དེའང་དག་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་ལས་ཐ་དད་དུ་དག་ཚུལ་གཞན་མེད་དེ་འདི་ལྟར་སྣང་ཚུལ་ལ་ནི་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཇེ་དག་ཏུ་སོང་བ་དང་ཡུལ་ཡང་གསར་དུ་དག་པར་སྣང་བ་ལྟར་ཡོད་ཀྱང་། གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་ནི་ཡུལ་གཟུགས༷་སོགས་ཀྱི༷་རང་བཞིན་ཡེ་ནས་དག༷་པ༷་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཉིད་ཡུལ་ཅན་གློ་བུར་གྱི་དྲི་མ་ལས་གྲོལ་བ་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་ཡེ་དག༷་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་པར༷་ཤེས༷་པར༷་བྱ༷་སྟེ། དེ་གཉིས་ཡེ་ནས་ཡུལ་ཡུལ་ཅན་གཉིས་སུ་མེད་པར་དག་པ་ཆེན་པོར་གནས་པའི་གནད་ལ་དོན་གཅིག་པས་དག་པ་དེ་གཉིས་ངོ་བོ་ཐ་མི་དད་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་དག་པ་དང་གཟུགས༷་སོགས་ཀྱི་དག༷་པ་དེ་ཉིད་གློ་བུར་བྲལ་དག་གི་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་སྒྲིབ་གཉིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤང་པའི་ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཐམ༷ས་ཅ༷ད་མཁྱེན༷་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཉི༷ད་ཀྱི་དག༷་པར༷་འགྱུར༷་ཏེ་དག་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྩ་བ་རང་བཞིན་རྣམ་དག་གི་དོན་ལ་གནད་གཅིག་པ་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་དག་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་ཐམ༷ས་ཅ༷ད་མཁྱེན༷་པ་ཉི༷ད་ཀྱི་དག་པ་དང་། གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་ལམ་སོ་སོའི་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་ཐོབ་པའི་དག༷་པ་དང༷་། གཞི་གཟུགས༷་སོགས་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དག༷་པ༷་གསུམ་པོ་འདི་ནི་སྣང་ཚུལ་ལ་ཐ་དད་དུ་བཞག་ཀྱང་། གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་ནམ༷་མཁའི༷་ཁ༷མས་ལ་ཐ་དད་མེད་པ་དང༷་མཚུངས༷་ཏེ༷་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་གཅིག་གི་ངོ་བོར་དབྱེ༷ར་མེ༷ད་ལ་བློས་ཀྱང་ཐ་དད་དུ་གཅ༷ད་དུ༷་མེ༷ད་དེ། ཆོས་ཉིད་རྣམ་དག་དེའི་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་གཟིགས་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོར། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་མངོན་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ་གདོད་ནས་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་གཟིགས་ཀྱི་མ་དག་པ་མེད་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའང་གློ་བུར་གྱི་དྲི་མ་བག་ཆགས་དང་བཅས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་མཐའ་དག་གཏན་ནས་སྤངས་པའི་དག་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་ཡིན་པས། དེས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟིགས་པ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡུལ་དང་ཡུལ་ཅན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གཉིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་མེད་པར་གཉིས་མེད་མཉམ་པ་ཆེན་པོར་ཡེ་ནས་དག་ཅིང་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་ཉིད་དུ་དབྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་རོ་གཅིག་ཏུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་དགོངས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་ཡིན་ལ། གཤིས་རྣལ་མ་དེའི་དོན་བབ་ཀྱིས་ཅོག་བཞག་ཏུ་སྐྱོང་བའི་ཚུལ་ཡང་། འདི་ལ་བསལ་བྱ་ཅི་ཡང་མེད། །བཞག་པར་བྱ་བ་གང་ཡང་མེད། །ཡང་དག་ཉིད་ལ་ཡང་དག་བལྟ། །ཡང་དག་མཐོང་ནས་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ། །ཞེས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
[1-152] translation already produced for this document:
The essence of the completely pure wakefulness. First, regarding the essence, there is one stanza starting with "the purity of form": all dharmas are primordially completely pure, naturally passed beyond suffering, fully awakened, naturally luminous, and primordially unarisen and unceasing; through this essence of equality, meditating on everything as having a single flavor in the single sphere, the great dharmadhātu, luminous and free from obscurations, is the essence of the wakefulness of meditative equipoise. If one asks what its manner is: illustrated here by the words "the purity of form," all dharmas, from form as an object of knowledge up to omniscience, are primordially unestablished in any dualistic nature such as apprehended and apprehender, completely afflicted and completely purified, self and other, entity and non-entity, and so forth; and although they exist as the single sphere of the dharmadhātu, primordially free from arising and ceasing, as the equality that is naturally completely pure and the great state free from obscurations, when adventitious delusion that fails to realize this arises, for the defiled mind that imputes self and dharmas, the objects appear as impure, and since the mind apprehends them as such, those who have defilements and obscurations on the side of complete affliction are called impure sentient beings. By entering the paths of the three vehicles taught in order to clear away those adventitious defilements, from the manner of seeing the true nature of dharmatā, which is naturally completely pure, more and more clearly, realizations arise—such as the four fruits of the śrāvakas, the fruit of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of seeing of the bodhisattvas, and the nine bhūmis of the path of meditation—and from the aspect of abandoning the defilements to be abandoned, they are called small, medium, and great purity; and those are called sentient beings pure of whatever defilements. Furthermore, although the nature of objects such as form has primordially never been impure, in accordance with the stages of purifying the adventitious defilements of apprehending them erroneously, just as when an eye defect is cleared away one sees objects more clearly, that subject sees the purity of the object, and through the power of seeing that, the subject is also called pure, but other than that there is no separate way of being pure; thus, although in the mode of appearance it seems that the subject becomes increasingly pure and the object also appears to be newly purified, in the mode of abiding, one "should" "know" "that" seeing that the nature "of" objects such as "form" is primordially "pure" is itself the subject's release from adventitious defilements, the primordial "purity" of the "fruit". Since those two share the same crucial point of primordially abiding in great purity without duality of object and subject, one should know that those two purities are indivisible in essence. Likewise, the purity of the "fruit" and the "purity" of "form" and so forth "become" the "purity" "of" "omniscient" wakefulness "itself", which is completely pure, having thoroughly abandoned the two obscurations, the culmination of the purity of separation from the adventitious; and all those purities share the same root crucial point in the meaning of natural complete purity, just as explained a moment ago. Thus, the ultimate purity, the purity of "omniscience" "itself", "and" the temporary "purity" of attaining the "fruit" of the various paths, and the "purity" of the basic "form" and so forth, the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources—although these three are posited as distinct in the mode of appearance, in the mode of abiding they "are like" the "element" "of space", which has no distinctness. They are "indivisible" within the single essence of the naturally completely pure dharmadhātu, and "cannot" be "divided" as distinct even by the mind. For the wakefulness of a buddha, which directly sees the nature of that completely pure dharmatā exactly as it is, all dharmas are seen as fully awakened or as primordially passed beyond suffering by nature; there is nothing impure. And since that wakefulness which realizes this is also the ultimate purity that has permanently abandoned all obscurations along with the latencies of adventitious defilements, to know that just as it sees, all dharmas are unestablished as the nature of dualistic phenomena such as object and subject, but are a single flavor, undifferentiated in being primordially pure and fully awakened in the great non-dual equality—this is the ultimate intent of the perfection of wisdom. And the manner of sustaining the meaning of that genuine condition by naturally resting effortlessly, one should understand in accordance with this statement: "In this there is nothing to be removed; / There is nothing whatsoever to be posited. / Look genuinely at the genuine itself. / Seeing genuinely, one is completely liberated."

heading: **མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའི་རྣམ་པར་དམིགས་མེད་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Fourth, teaching the aspect of that wakefulness of meditative equipoise as objectless. There is one stanza starting with "all dharmas": Thus, since "all" "dharmas" subsumed by affliction and purification are by their own essence "pure" of the "nature" of afflictions, "and" since the observation of objects of knowledge has become "completely" "pure", if "bodhisattvas" "observe" and abide in the supreme meaning of the "perfection" "of" "wisdom" which realizes the nature of things to be exactly like that, the observer, the "one" "who" "meditates" on the perfection of wisdom, is "not" "observed", and "all" "dharmas" to be observed are also "not" "observed"; abiding in the expanse where proliferations are pacified, "this" "is" "engaging" in the "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom". The approach of the extensive teaching.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-161] source:
གསུམ་པ་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ལ། སྦྱོར་བ་ལ་བསླབ་པའི་རིམ་པ་དང་། སྦྱོར་བ་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཚུལ་དང་། དེ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་པོ་གང་ཟག་བསྟན་པ་དང་། དེ་ལྟར་འཇུག་པའི་གང་ཟག་གི་ཆེ་བ་དང་། དེས་བསླབ་བྱ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཆེ་བ་དང་ལྔ་ལས་དང་པོ་ལ
[1-161] translation already produced for this document:
Third, regarding the approach of the extensive teaching, there are five parts: the stages of training in the application; the way the result of that application is genuinely established; teaching the person who applies themselves to that; the greatness of the person who enters in that way; and the greatness of the dharma they train in. From among these five, regarding the first:

[1-162] source:
། ༈སྦྱོར་བ་ལ་བསླབ་པའི་རིམ་པ། བསྒོམ་བྱ་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ། སྦྱོར་བ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། བར་དུ་གཅོད་པའི་སྐྱོན། སྦྱོར་བའི་བྱེད་ལས། རྐྱེན་བཤེས་གཉེན་བཤད་པ་དང་ལྔ
[1-162] translation already produced for this document:
The stages of training in the application. There are five parts: the essence of the application to be meditated upon; the benefits arising from meditating on the application; the faults that cause interruptions; the function of the application; and explaining the condition, the spiritual friend.

[1-163] source:
། ༈བསྒོམ་བྱ་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ། དང་པོ། རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ནི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། རྒྱལ༷་བ༷་མི་ཡི་སེང་གེ་ལ༷་ནི༷་ལྷ༷་ཡི་རྒྱལ༷་པོ་བརྒྱ༷་བྱི༷ན་གྱིས༷་ཞུས༷་པ༷། གང་ཞིག་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་བྱ་བ་བྱས་ཤིང་དེ་ལས་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས༷་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྤྱོ༷ད་པ༷་ལ་ཇི༷་ལྟར༷་བརྩོན༷་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པའི་ལན་དུ་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། ཕུང༷་པོ༷་དང་ཁ༷མས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་ལ༷་རྡུལ༷་ཙམ༷་དུའང་དམིགས་པ་དང་གནས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བརྩོན༷་པར༷་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་། ཕུང༷་པོ༷་ལ་སོགས་པར་མི་དམིགས་མི་གནས་མི༷་བརྩོན༷་ལ་དེ༷་ནི༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་དག་གི་ཡང་དག་པའི་བརྩོན༷་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །༈སྦྱོར་བ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན།
[1-163] translation already produced for this document:
The essence of the application to be meditated upon. First, there is one stanza starting with "To the victor": "To" the "victor", the lion of men, "Śakra", the "king" "of" the "gods", "asked": "How" should the "bodhisattvas" who have served the past victors, who have generated the roots of virtue from that, and who are guided by spiritual friends, "exert" themselves in "engaging" in the perfection of "wisdom"? In response to this question, he declared: they "do" "not" "exert" themselves by way of observing or abiding even to the slightest degree in the dharmas subsumed by the "aggregates" and elements, "and" "not" observing, not abiding, and "not" "exerting" themselves in the "aggregates" and so forth, "that" "is" the genuine "exertion" of the "bodhisattvas". The benefits arising from meditating on the application.

[1-164] source:
གཉིས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ། སྦྱོར་བའི་རྒྱུ་གུས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སྦྱོར་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་འབྲས་བུའི་ཡོན་ཏན། གནས་སྐབས་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གསུམ།
[1-164] translation already produced for this document:
Second, regarding the benefits, there are three parts: the benefit of respect, which is the cause of the application; the benefit of the result arising from the application; and the benefit of the essence of the application on the occasion.

[1-165] source:
དང་པོ། གང་ཞིག་ཆོས་འདི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། གང་ཟག་གང༷་ཞིག༷་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་གཞུང་འདི་ནས་ཆོས༷་འདི༷་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ངོ་བོ་མེད་ཀྱང་རྣམ་པ་མི་འགག་པ་སྦྲུལ༷་པ་དང༷་སྒྱུ༷་མ༷་འདྲ༷་བར་བཤད་པ་ཐོས༷་ནས༷། དེའི་དོན་ལ་སོམས༷་ཉི༷་མེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་ཡིད་ཆེས་ནས་དེ་སློབ༷་པ་ལ༷་ཕྱིར༷་ཞིང༷་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་སྦྱོར༷་བར་བྱེ༷ད་པ༷་ཡི་སེམ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་དེ༷་ནི༷་སྔོན་ཡུན་རིང༷་པོ་ནས༷་ཐེག༷་ཆེན༷་ལ་ཞུགས༷་པ་ཉིད་དུ་རིག༷་པར་བྱ༷་ཞིང་དེས་སྔོན་སངས༷་རྒྱས༷་བྱེ༷་བ༷་ཁྲག༷་ཁྲི༷ག་མང༷་པོ་ལ༷་མཆོད་ཅིང་རྗེད་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལྷག༷་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས༷་པ་ཡི༷ན་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་འདྲའི་རྒྱུ་སྔོན་སོང་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ཐོས་ནས་མོས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མི་འབྱུང་ངོ་། །
[1-165] translation already produced for this document:
First, there is one stanza starting with "Whichever [sentient being] ... this dharma": "Whichever" person, "having heard" it explained from this text of the perfection of wisdom that "these" "dharmas" all lack an essence but their aspects are unceasing, "like" an "emanation" "and" an "illusion", has "no" "doubt" about its meaning and, with conviction, "furthermore" earnestly "applies" themselves "to" "training" in it—"that" "sentient being" "should be known" to have "entered" the Mahāyāna "long" "ago" in the past, and "should be known" to "have" exceedingly "served" "many" "tens of millions" and hundreds of billions of "buddhas" in the past by way of honoring and revering them and so forth; for, without relying on such a pre-existing cause, one does not become inclined toward the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom upon hearing it.

[1-166] source:
གཉིས་པ་ལ་བར་ཆད་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སྐུ་གསུམ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གཉིས།
[1-166] translation already produced for this document:
Second, there are two parts: the benefit of not being harmed by interruptions, and the benefit of attaining the three kāyas.

heading: **སྐུ་གསུམ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: Second, there are three parts: the benefit of attaining the dharmakāya; the benefit of attaining the saṃbhogakāya; and the benefit of attaining the nirmāṇakāya.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[1-171] source:
གསུམ་པ་སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་ཐོབ་ཚུལ། དཔེར་ན་བུད་མེད་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། དཔེར༷་ན༷་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་མངལ་ཆགས་པའི་སྦྲུམ༷་མ་གང༷་ཞིག་མངལ་གྱི་ཟླ་དུས་རྫོགས་ནས་བཙའ་བའི་ནད་ཀྱི་སྡུག༷་བསྔལ༷་མྱོང་བས་ཉེན༷་པར་གྱུར༷་པ་ན༷། ཚུལ་དེ༷་ནི༷་དེ༷་ཡི༷་བཙའ༷་བའི༷་དུས༷་ལ༷་བབ༷་པའི་ཚོད་ཅེས༷་བྱ༷་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་གང་ཞིག་རྒྱལ༷་བའི༷་ཤེས༷་ར༷བ་འདི་ཉན༷་པ་ཐོབ་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་ཡིད་དང་བའི་དགའ༷་བ་དང༷་འདོད་པའི་འདུན༷་པ༷་བསྐྱེ༷ད་པ༷་ནི་མྱུར༷་དུ༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་རེག༷་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ།ལམ་འདི་ལས་རིགས་ཀྱི་ས་བོན་གསོས་བཏབ་ནས་ཚོགས་རྫོགས་པར་བྱས་ཏེ་སྦྲུམ་མ་ལས་བུ་བཙས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སྐུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་དངོས་སུ་སྣང༷་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

Third, the way of attaining the nirmāṇakāya. There is one stanza starting with "For example, a woman": "For example", "when" "a" pregnant "woman" who has conceived "experiences" the "suffering" of the pains of giving birth and is "afflicted" because the months in the womb are complete, that state "is" what is "called" "the" "time" "having" "come" "for" "her" "to" "give" "birth". "Likewise", "any" "bodhisattva" who attains the "hearing" of "this" "wisdom" "of" "the" "victor" "and" "generates" a clear mind of "joy" "and" the "desire" to attain it "will" "swiftly" "touch" great "awakening"; for through this path, having nourished the seed of the disposition and completed the accumulations, just as a child is born from a pregnant woman, the nirmāṇakāya "will" "manifest" in actuality in the world.

Third, the benefits of the essence. There are two parts: although one does not conceptualize increase, decrease, and so forth, one does not touch the one-sided extreme of nirvāṇa; and although one is free from conceptualization, one accomplishes the benefit of beings.

[1-173] source:
དང་པོ། ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་གི་དོན་ལ་ཚུལ་བཞིན་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་ཚེ༷་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་གི་རྣལ༷་འབྱོར༷་པ༷་དེས་གཟུགས༷་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི༷་འཕེལ༷་བ༷་སྟེ་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་རྒྱུན་བསགས་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དང༷་ནི༷། ཡོངས༷་སུ༷་འགྲིབ༷་པ་སྟེ་འགག་པ་དང་སྔར་ལས་དམའ་བར་གྱུར་པའི་ཚུལ་མི༷་མཐོང༷་སྟེ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་དུ་འཕེལ་འགྲིབ་བྲི་གང་དང་བྲལ་ཏེ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གནས་པའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གང༷་ཞིག༷་ཆོས༷་དགེ་བ་དང༷་ཆོས༷་མིན༷་མི་དགེ་བ་དང་། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དམ་ཆོས༷་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས༷་ཞེས་སུའང་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་མི༷་མཐོང༷་བས་དམིགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་ཞིང༷་སྤྲོས་པ་མེད་པ་ལ་གནས་ན་ཡང་། ཞི་བའི་དབྱིངས་འབའ་ཞིག་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པའི་མྱ༷་ངན༷་འདས༷་པ་ལ༷་མ༷་རེག༷་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ༷་ནི༷་སྲིད་ཞིའི་མཐར་མི་གནས་པའི་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་ལ་གན༷ས་པའོ། །

[1-174] source:
གཉིས་པ་གང་ཞིག་འདིར་སྤྱོད་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། གང༷་ཞིག༷་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདིར༷་ཚུལ་བཞིན་སྤྱོ༷ད་པ་དེ་ནི་སངས༷་རྒྱས༷་ཀྱི་ཆོས༷་སྟོབས་སོགས་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་དེར་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པས་རྣམ་པར་མི༷་རྟོག༷་སྟེ༷། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལམ་སྟོབ༷ས་ལྔ་དང༷་རྫུ༷་འཕྲུལ༷་གྱི་རྐང༷་པ༷་བཞི་སོགས་དང་འབྲས་བུའམ་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཞི༷་བ་ལ་ཡང་རྣམ་པར་མི༷་རྟོག༷ གཟུགས་སོགས་ཕུང་ཁམས་རྣམས་ལའང་རྣམ༷་པར༷་མི༷་རྟོག༷་གོ་ཞེས། དོན་ལ་འདིས་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པའི་མཚན་མ་བཞི་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་གཟུངས་བསྟན་པ་ལས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་གོ་རིམ་བསྡེབ་ན། ཕུང་པོ་སོགས་འཁོར་བའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་པར་རྟོག་པ་དང་། ལམ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ལ་གཉེན་པོར་རྟོག་པ་དང་། དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་རྟོག་པ་དང་། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཐོབ་པར་རྟོག་པ་རྣམས་དང་བྲལ་བར་བསྟན་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ལྟར་རྟོག༷་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྲལ༷་ཡང་རྟོག་མེད་ལྷུན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་དེའི་མཐུ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཤུགས་སམ་བྱི༷ན་གྱི༷་རློབ༷ས་ཀྱིས༷་བདུད་འདུལ་བ་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་བྱ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབད་མེད་དུ་སྤྱོ༷ད་དེ། མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་འདི་ལ་གནས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་གཉིས་སུ་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པའི་མཐུ་ཐོབ་པས་དེའི་ཕྲིན་ལས་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་ཆུད་མི་ཟའོ། །ཚུལ་འདི༷་ལྟ་བུ་ནི༷་ཤེ༷ས་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་སྤྱོ༷ད་པ༷་ཡི༷ན་ནོ། །༈བར་དུ་གཅོད་པའི་སྐྱོན།

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Whoever practices here": "Whoever" properly "practices" "here" in the perfection of wisdom "does" "not" "conceptualize" even "the" "phenomena" "of" "a" "buddha", such as the powers and so forth, by fully apprehending them as this or that. "Likewise", "they" "do" "not" "conceptualize" the path, such as the five "powers" "and" the four "bases" "of" "miraculous" "power" and so forth, or the result or reality, the "peace" of "awakening". "They" "do" "not" "conceptualize" either the aggregates and elements such as form and so forth. In meaning, this teaches the way of being free from the four marks of conceptualization. As for how this is, if we arrange them in order according to what is taught in the Dhāraṇī of Entering Non-Conceptualization, it teaches freedom from conceptualizing the phenomena of saṃsāra, such as the aggregates and so forth, as having an inherent nature; conceptualizing the path of the perfection of wisdom as an antidote; conceptualizing reality as dharmatā; and conceptualizing the phenomena of a buddha as something to be attained. Thus, although "free" from all "conceptualization", through the power of that non-conceptual, spontaneously present samādhi and the force of aspiration, or by its "blessing", one effortlessly "practices" the taming of māras and all deeds for the benefit of others; for by abiding in this non-conceptual samādhi, one attains the power of being blessed by the buddhas in a non-dual manner through dharmatā, so its awakened activity is never wasted in the slightest. "Such" a way "is" "the" "practice" of the non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom". The faults of interruption.

translation: First, there are one and a half stanzas starting with "Shows the world": "The world" refers to all the phenomena renowned as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, as many as there are, and whatever the nature of their conventional cause, effect, and essence may be, the perfection of wisdom "shows" them to her own sons, the buddhas; because relying upon this perfection of wisdom, the "mother" "who gives birth" "to the" "victors", those buddhas see those phenomena as if placing a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. Thus, with these one and a half stanzas, it is said that, in short, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, all the phenomenal modes of the two truths have come to be seen by the buddhas.

First, there are one and a half stanzas starting with "Shows the world": "The world" refers to all the phenomena renowned as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, as many as there are, and whatever the nature of their conventional cause, effect, and essence may be, the perfection of wisdom "shows" them to her own sons, the buddhas; because relying upon this perfection of wisdom, the "mother" "who gives birth" "to the" "victors", those buddhas see those phenomena as if placing a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. Thus, with these one and a half stanzas, it is said that, in short, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, all the phenomenal modes of the two truths have come to be seen by the buddhas.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཉིས་པ་ལ་གཞི་འཁོར་འདས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་མཁྱེན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་མཛད་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ། ལམ་མཐའ་གཉིས་འགོག་པའི་ཚུལ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་གསུམ

Second, there are three parts: joining to the knowledge of the mode of the basis, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; joining to the deeds of the fruition, omniscience; and joining to the method of blocking the two extremes of the path.

[1-199] source:
། ༈གཞི་འཁོར་འདས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་མཁྱེན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ། དང་པོ་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བདེན་གཉིས་ལ་མཁས་པ་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པས་མཚན་ཐོབ་པ་གཉིས།
[1-199] translation already produced for this document:
Joining to the knowledge of the mode of the basis, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. First, there are two parts: relying upon the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in the two truths of the world, and attaining the name through realizing suchness.

[1-200] source:
དང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་ཕྱེད་དང་གཉིས་ཏེ། འཇིག༷་རྟེན༷་ནི་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་རྣམས་ཏེ་དེ་དག་གི་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་ངོ་བོའི་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་རང་གི་སྲས་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ལ་སྟོན༷་པ༷་སྟེ། རྒྱལ༷་བ༷་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱི༷་སྐྱེ༷ད་བྱེ༷ད་ཀྱི་ཡུམ༷་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་དེ་དག་གིས་ཆོས་དེ་དག་སྐྱུ་རུ་ར་རློན་པ་ལག་མཐིལ་ཏུ་བཞག་པ་བཞིན་དུ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཞན་ཡང་གདུལ་བྱའི་དོན་མཛད་པ་ལ་དགོས་པ་ཆེད་དུ་བཀར་ཏེ་སེམ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་གཞན༷་གྱི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱི༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པ༷་ནང་དུ་བསྡུས་པ་དང་ཕྱིར་གཡེང་བ་དང་ཆགས་བཅས་དང་ཆགས་བྲལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མཐའ་མེད་པ་དག་ཀྱང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་གོམས་པའི་མཐུས་རང་གི་སྲས་ལ་སྟོན༷་པར༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་སྟོན་པ་དང་། འཇིག༷་རྟེན༷་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་དང༷་། དགྲ༷་བཅོ༷མ་པའི་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་དང་རང༷༷་རྒྱལ༷་གྱི་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་དང༷་། རྒྱལ༷་སྲས༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་དག་ནི་ཐ་དད་དུ་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཅི༷ག་པ༷་ཉི༷ད་དེ༷། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དངོས༷་པོ་དང་བྲལ༷་བའི་ཕྱིར་ན་གཞན་དང་གཞན༷་དུ་ཡོད་པ་མི༷ན་པས་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་ཅེས་བྱ་ལ། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ༷་ནི་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་གཤེ༷གས་པས༷་མཁྱེན༷་ཅིང་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཤོ་ལོ་ཀ་ཕྱེད་དང་གཉིས་པོ་འདིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མདོར་ན་བདེན་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཚུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་གཟིགས་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ་ཞེས་སོ། །
[1-200] translation already produced for this document:
First, there are one and a half stanzas starting with "Shows the world": "The world" refers to all the phenomena renowned as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, as many as there are, and whatever the nature of their conventional cause, effect, and essence may be, the perfection of wisdom "shows" them to her own sons, the buddhas; because relying upon this perfection of wisdom, the "mother" "who gives birth" "to the" "victors", those buddhas see those phenomena as if placing a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. Thus, with these one and a half stanzas, it is said that, in short, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, all the phenomenal modes of the two truths have come to be seen by the buddhas.

[1-201] source:
གཉིས་པ། མཁས་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། ཇི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ཡང་མས་བུ་ལ་མིང་འདོགས་པ་ལྟར་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་པའི་མཚན་ཐོབ་པ་ནི། དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས༷་པ༷་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་འཇིག༷་རྟེན༷་གྱི་ཁམས་འདིར་འཚོ་གཞེས་ཤིང་གན༷ས་སམ༷་མྱ༷་ངན༷་ལས་འདས༷་ཀྱང༷་རུང༷་སྟེ། ཆོས༷་ཉི༷ད་སྐྱོན༷་མེ༷ད་པ་གང་ཞིག་ཆོས༷་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱི་སྟོང༷་པ༷་ཉིད་དུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི༷་ནི་ནམ་ཡང་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་པ་དང་སུས་ཀྱང་དཀྲུགས་པར་མི་ནུས་པར་ནམ་མཁའ་བཞིན་དུ་གན༷ས་སྟེ༷། བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་ཉི༷ད་ཡེ་ནས་བབ་ཀྱིས་གནས་པ་འདི༷་ཡི་ཡིན་ལུགས་མ་ནོར་བར་བློས་རྗེས༷་སུ༷་རྟོགས༷་ཤིང་ནམ་ཞིག་རྟོགས་པ་མཐར་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཚེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གཤེགས་པའམ་རྟོགས་པ་དེ༷་ཡི་ཕྱིར༷་ན་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་གཤེ༷གས་པ་ཞེས༷་སངས༷་རྒྱས༷་རྣམས་ལ་མཚ༷ན་དུ་གསོལ༷་བར་གྱུར༷་ཏོ། །༈འབྲས་བུ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་མཛད་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ།
[1-201] translation already produced for this document:
Second, there is one stanza starting with "The wise [...] the world": Just as in the world a mother gives a name to her son, attaining the name "tathāgata" in reliance upon the Mother of the Victors is as follows: Whether the buddhas, "wise" in reality, "abide" living in this "world" realm "or" pass into "nirvāṇa", this "flawless" "dharmatā", which is expressed as the "emptiness" "of phenomena", "abides" like space, never changing and incapable of being disturbed by anyone; "bodhisattvas" mentally "realize" unmistakably the mode of being of "this" "suchness" which abides naturally from the beginning, and when eventually their realization reaches perfection, "because" they have gone or realized in accordance with suchness, the "buddhas" have been "bestowed with the name" "tathāgata". Joining to the deeds of the fruition, omniscience.

[1-202] source:
གཉིས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་ལ་སྦྱོར་ཚུལ་ལ། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དོན་གཉིས་འགྲུབ་པ་དང་། ཁྱད་པར་དུ་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པའི་ཚུལ་གཉིས།
[1-202] translation already produced for this document:

Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. First, there are one and a half stanzas starting with "Shows the world": "The world" refers to all the phenomena renowned as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, as many as there are, and whatever the nature of their conventional cause, effect, and essence may be, the perfection of wisdom "shows" them to her own sons, the buddhas; because relying upon this perfection of wisdom, the "mother" "who gives birth" "to the" "victors", those buddhas see those phenomena as if placing a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. Thus, with these one and a half stanzas, it is said that, in short, relying upon the perfection of wisdom, all the phenomenal modes of the two truths have come to be seen by the buddhas.

First, there is one stanza starting with "Perfection of wisdom": Since limitless undefiled "joy" arises if one abides in the "perfection of wisdom", it is like the joyful "grove" of the gods; "relying upon" and "abiding" in it, the "domain of experience" of the "guides", the "buddhas" who possess the "ten powers", "is like this": If one asks what that is, even though they "completely extract" limitless "sentient beings" "from" various "suffering" and the "three lower realms", for "those" buddhas there "never" "arises" the "concept" of "sentient beings", because with great objectless compassion they perform the teaching of Dharma and so forth through constant, all-pervasive, and spontaneously accomplished enlightened activity.

heading: **དོན།**
translation: First, there is one stanza starting with "Not seeing forms": Because "forms" lack their own essence, they are objectless or "not" "seen". Likewise, "feelings" "too" are "not" "seen", "and" "discriminations" are "not" "seen", "and" "mental formations" are "not" "seen"; in the domain of experience resting in equipoise on reality, "wherever" one looks, there is "nothing" "seen" that is the basis for what is called "consciousness", "and" what is called "mind", and what is called "mentality". Regarding this, it is explained in other commentaries that they are expressed in this way from the perspective of mind engaging the past, consciousness engaging the future, and mentality functioning in the present, or they are expressed as synonyms; whereas Jñānapāda states that, as is widely renowned, mind is the all-ground consciousness, mentality is the afflicted mentality, and consciousness refers to the six engaging consciousnesses. Thus, since all phenomena, as represented by the five aggregates, are objectless, not seeing them as the essence of anything whatsoever—"this" "is" "seeing" the genuine nature "of phenomena", "taught" the "Tathāgata", just as flawless eyes not seeing floaters is seeing the nature of floaters.

First, there are one and a half stanzas starting with "Shows the world": "The world" refers to all the phenomena renowned as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, as many as there are, and whatever the nature of their conventional cause, effect, and essence may be, the perfection of wisdom "shows" them to her own sons, the buddhas; because relying upon this perfection of wisdom, the "mother" "who gives birth" "to the" "victors", those buddhas see those phenomena as if placing a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, making the purpose specific for performing the benefit of those to be tamed, even the boundless "behavior" "of the minds" "of others", "sentient" "beings" of limitless realms, as many as there are—such as minds drawn inward, scattered outward, with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth without end—she "shows" to her own sons by the power of their familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is showing the relative truth. The "suchness" "of" the "world", the five aggregates, "and" the "suchness" "of arhats", and the "suchness" of "pratyekabuddhas" "and" the "suchness" of the "victors' sons", the bodhisattvas, are "one" because they are not established as different; since they are all "free" from "substantial entities", they are "not" existent as other and "other", thus they are called "suchness". The "perfection of wisdom", which is the abiding mode of all such phenomena of thorough affliction and purification, this suchness, the "tathāgatas" "know" and comprehend it just as it is. translation: Second, there is one stanza starting with "Seeing space": What is the example for that seeing of what is not seen? By doing so, you will understand that the mere non-seeing of any corporeal phenomenon is designated as seeing space. "Like" "that" example, what is called "seeing" the reality "of phenomena" is also "taught" by the "Tathāgata" as seeing phenomena when, having known with the eye of wisdom that no phenomenon whatsoever is established, one does not observe or see them as the essence of anything whatsoever. translation: First, there is one stanza starting with "Whoever [...] Sugatas": "Whoever" among persons "has" "firm" and irreversible "faith" of belief and longing toward the "Sugatas" and their sons, the "bodhisattvas", "and" who "intends" upon—seeking out through intention—and "endeavours" through "application" in the "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom", which is the path to become a bodhisattva and a Buddha, is replete with both method and wisdom; therefore, "having" "thoroughly" "passed" "beyond" the mistaken paths of the "two" "grounds" "of" "śrāvakas" "and" "pratyekabuddhas", they "will" "swiftly" "attain" the holy "enlightenment" "of" a "Jina", which is "not" "overcome" by the obscurations of existence and peace. Thus, faith in the supreme vehicle is the initial door of entry, and wisdom ensures that one does not decline from attaining the fruit in accordance with faith; hence, these two, method and wisdom, are primarily taught. Although beginners may have faith, if they lack the perfection of wisdom, it is possible for them to decline from the path; however, once the intent of the profound perfection of wisdom has been assimilated into their experience, they attain unassailable faith, and it is impossible to decline from the path.

First, there is one stanza starting with "Those endowed with great renown": Whoever has entered the Mahāyāna, the path that is supremely profound and vast, "those" who are "endowed" with "great" "renown" of the name 'bodhisattva' in the infinite fields of the Jinas "don" the "armor" of what is "difficult" "to" "do". Thus, they generate the mind, saying, "I shall cause all infinite sentient beings, equal to space in conventional terms, to transcend sorrow into the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa", and furthermore, they are free from apprehending affliction and purification, so thus they "do" "not" don the "armor" that apprehends as entities the "aggregates", "and" "elements", "and" "sense" "sources", and they are "free" from the "perception" of clinging to the "three" "vehicles", "and" they abide in the perfection of wisdom "without" any dharmas whatsoever being "completely" apprehended or "grasped". Exactly because of that, since they trust in the profound meaning, they "do" "not" "turn" "back" from attaining the fruit of perfect enlightenment endowed with the three great purposes, "and" they are "unwavering" elsewhere from the method of the Mahāyāna path, and since their mindstream cannot be afflicted by any adverse condition, māra or opponent, they "are" "of" the "nature" of being "undisturbed". This is as it is spoken in the extensive sutra: "Bhagavān, those bodhisattvas who don the armor to cause all sentient beings to transcend sorrow, yet who do not apprehend sentient beings, are doing what is difficult," and "Subhūti, that armor is not connected to form," and so forth.

heading: **སྤྱད་བྱའི་ཆོས་ཟབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: First, there is one stanza starting with "Of the guides": "This" "dharma" of the perfect Buddhas, the "guides", the Great Mother, is supremely "profound"; all foundational dharmas are non-arising and, being mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, and so because they have primordially transcended the domain of the grasped and the grasping mind, they are "difficult" "to" "see". Therefore, during the phase of the path it is "not" "realized" "by" "anyone", "and" at the time of the fruit it is "not" something that "will" "be" "attained". If it were to exist in the nature of something realized and attained, it would not be suitable as genuine realization and attainment; this is just as is stated again and again in other sūtras as well, in the manner of: "Since enlightenment was not found even by the Buddha himself, what need to speak of others? Because the nature of enlightenment is primordially isolated." Since this profound dharmatā of no seeing, no realization, and no attainment is profound and difficult to fathom, "therefore", "having" "found" the great unexcelled "enlightenment", the "compassionate" perfect Buddha who "performs" "benefit" for all sentient beings "showed" "little" "inclination" to teach the dharma, thinking, "In the multitude of 'sentient' 'beings', 'who' could 'know' 'this' kind of profound dharma that 'I' have realized?" And as it is said in the Lalitavistara: "Profound, peaceful, free from fabrication, luminous, unconditioned, / I have found a dharma that is like nectar. / Yet to whomever I teach it, they will not understand it, / So I will remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is also said in the Mūlaprajñā: "Therefore, having known that the depth / Of this dharma is difficult for the weak to realize, / The Muni's mind / Completely turned away from teaching the dharma."

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Acting in that way": "Those" "moons" "of" "speech", who are the spiritual friends of the Mahāyāna "acting" "in" "that" "way", that is, who "well" teach the instructions, and who have become a great "ocean" of good qualities that are difficult to realize, endowed with the light rays of the genuine dharma, "are" a "refuge" who dispel the suffering "of" "beings" by teaching the dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, "and" an "ally" who establishes them in the happiness of nirvāṇa, "and" a "haven" who dispels the causes of suffering. First, there is one stanza starting with "Those endowed with great renown": Whoever has entered the Mahāyāna, the path that is supremely profound and vast, "those" who are "endowed" with "great" "renown" of the name 'bodhisattva' in the infinite fields of the Jinas "don" the "armor" of what is "difficult" "to" "do". Thus, they generate the mind, saying, "I shall cause all infinite sentient beings, equal to space in conventional terms, to transcend sorrow into the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa", and furthermore, they are free from apprehending affliction and purification, so thus they "do" "not" don the "armor" that apprehends as entities the "aggregates", "and" "elements", "and" "sense" "sources", and they are "free" from the "perception" of clinging to the "three" "vehicles", "and" they abide in the perfection of wisdom "without" any dharmas whatsoever being "completely" apprehended or "grasped". Exactly because of that, since they trust in the profound meaning, they "do" "not" "turn" "back" from attaining the fruit of perfect enlightenment endowed with the three great purposes, "and" they are "unwavering" elsewhere from the method of the Mahāyāna path, and since their mindstream cannot be afflicted by any adverse condition, māra or opponent, they "are" "of" the "nature" of being "undisturbed". This is as it is spoken in the extensive sutra: "Bhagavān, those bodhisattvas who don the armor to cause all sentient beings to transcend sorrow, yet who do not apprehend sentient beings, are doing what is difficult," and "Subhūti, that armor is not connected to form," and so forth.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་ཟབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན།**
translation: Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

First, there is one stanza starting with "Of the guides": "This" "dharma" of the perfect Buddhas, the "guides", the Great Mother, is supremely "profound"; all foundational dharmas are non-arising and, being mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, and so because they have primordially transcended the domain of the grasped and the grasping mind, they are "difficult" "to" "see". Therefore, during the phase of the path it is "not" "realized" "by" "anyone", "and" at the time of the fruit it is "not" something that "will" "be" "attained". If it were to exist in the nature of something realized and attained, it would not be suitable as genuine realization and attainment; this is just as is stated again and again in other sūtras as well, in the manner of: "Since enlightenment was not found even by the Buddha himself, what need to speak of others? Because the nature of enlightenment is primordially isolated." Since this profound dharmatā of no seeing, no realization, and no attainment is profound and difficult to fathom, "therefore", "having" "found" the great unexcelled "enlightenment", the "compassionate" perfect Buddha who "performs" "benefit" for all sentient beings "showed" "little" "inclination" to teach the dharma, thinking, "In the multitude of 'sentient' 'beings', 'who' could 'know' 'this' kind of profound dharma that 'I' have realized?" And as it is said in the Lalitavistara: "Profound, peaceful, free from fabrication, luminous, unconditioned, / I have found a dharma that is like nectar. / Yet to whomever I teach it, they will not understand it, / So I will remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is also said in the Mūlaprajñā: "Therefore, having known that the depth / Of this dharma is difficult for the weak to realize, / The Muni's mind / Completely turned away from teaching the dharma."

First, there is one stanza starting with "Of the guides": "This" "dharma" of the perfect Buddhas, the "guides", the Great Mother, is supremely "profound"; all foundational dharmas are non-arising and, being mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, and so because they have primordially transcended the domain of the grasped and the grasping mind, they are "difficult" "to" "see". Therefore, during the phase of the path it is "not" "realized" "by" "anyone", "and" at the time of the fruit it is "not" something that "will" "be" "attained". If it were to exist in the nature of something realized and attained, it would not be suitable as genuine realization and attainment; this is just as is stated again and again in other sūtras as well, in the manner of: "Since enlightenment was not found even by the Buddha himself, what need to speak of others? Because the nature of enlightenment is primordially isolated." Since this profound dharmatā of no seeing, no realization, and no attainment is profound and difficult to fathom, "therefore", "having" "found" the great unexcelled "enlightenment", the "compassionate" perfect Buddha who "performs" "benefit" for all sentient beings "showed" "little" "inclination" to teach the dharma, thinking, "In the multitude of 'sentient' 'beings', 'who' could 'know' 'this' kind of profound dharma that 'I' have realized?" And as it is said in the Lalitavistara: "Profound, peaceful, free from fabrication, luminous, unconditioned, / I have found a dharma that is like nectar. / Yet to whomever I teach it, they will not understand it, / So I will remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is also said in the Mūlaprajñā: "Therefore, having known that the depth / Of this dharma is difficult for the weak to realize, / The Muni's mind / Completely turned away from teaching the dharma."

First, there is one stanza starting with "Of the guides": "This" "dharma" of the perfect Buddhas, the "guides", the Great Mother, is supremely "profound"; all foundational dharmas are non-arising and, being mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, and so because they have primordially transcended the domain of the grasped and the grasping mind, they are "difficult" "to" "see". Therefore, during the phase of the path it is "not" "realized" "by" "anyone", "and" at the time of the fruit it is "not" something that "will" "be" "attained". If it were to exist in the nature of something realized and attained, it would not be suitable as genuine realization and attainment; this is just as is stated again and again in other sūtras as well, in the manner of: "Since enlightenment was not found even by the Buddha himself, what need to speak of others? Because the nature of enlightenment is primordially isolated." Since this profound dharmatā of no seeing, no realization, and no attainment is profound and difficult to fathom, "therefore", "having" "found" the great unexcelled "enlightenment", the "compassionate" perfect Buddha who "performs" "benefit" for all sentient beings "showed" "little" "inclination" to teach the dharma, thinking, "In the multitude of 'sentient' 'beings', 'who' could 'know' 'this' kind of profound dharma that 'I' have realized?" And as it is said in the Lalitavistara: "Profound, peaceful, free from fabrication, luminous, unconditioned, / I have found a dharma that is like nectar. / Yet to whomever I teach it, they will not understand it, / So I will remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is also said in the Mūlaprajñā: "Therefore, having known that the depth / Of this dharma is difficult for the weak to realize, / The Muni's mind / Completely turned away from teaching the dharma."

Here, hesitation and so forth are just synonyms for doubt, teaching that they do not have any coarse or subtle doubts, such as those that are actively operating; alternatively, they can be viewed as distinct isolates, such as having no two-pointed mind regarding the path and fruit in the manner of "doubt" regarding the present, "hesitation" regarding the past, and "two-mindedness" regarding the future. By means of that trust free from doubt, having "heard" the profound "perfection" "of" "wisdom", their mind "does" "not" "shrink" "back" from its meaning, and since they have brought the profound dharma under their own experience through their own intellect, they "do" "not" "rely" "on" the "kindness" "of" "others", meaning that it is not the case that they lack certainty, relying on others and entering wherever they are led; and because they have become like that, one "should" "know" that they "do" "not" "turn" "back" from the path and fruit of the supreme vehicle.

First, there is one stanza starting with "Of the guides": "This" "dharma" of the perfect Buddhas, the "guides", the Great Mother, is supremely "profound"; all foundational dharmas are non-arising and, being mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, and so because they have primordially transcended the domain of the grasped and the grasping mind, they are "difficult" "to" "see". Therefore, during the phase of the path it is "not" "realized" "by" "anyone", "and" at the time of the fruit it is "not" something that "will" "be" "attained". If it were to exist in the nature of something realized and attained, it would not be suitable as genuine realization and attainment; this is just as is stated again and again in other sūtras as well, in the manner of: "Since enlightenment was not found even by the Buddha himself, what need to speak of others? Because the nature of enlightenment is primordially isolated." Since this profound dharmatā of no seeing, no realization, and no attainment is profound and difficult to fathom, "therefore", "having" "found" the great unexcelled "enlightenment", the "compassionate" perfect Buddha who "performs" "benefit" for all sentient beings "showed" "little" "inclination" to teach the dharma, thinking, "In the multitude of 'sentient' 'beings', 'who' could 'know' 'this' kind of profound dharma that 'I' have realized?" And as it is said in the Lalitavistara: "Profound, peaceful, free from fabrication, luminous, unconditioned, / I have found a dharma that is like nectar. / Yet to whomever I teach it, they will not understand it, / So I will remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is also said in the Mūlaprajñā: "Therefore, having known that the depth / Of this dharma is difficult for the weak to realize, / The Muni's mind / Completely turned away from teaching the dharma."

translation: Second, there is one stanza starting with "The suchness of the past": Just as in the example space has no distinctions, likewise, "whatever" is "the" "suchness" of dharmas of "the" "past" time, and "whatever" is "the" "suchness" of the "future", and "whatever" is "the" "suchness" of the "present", and whatever is the suchness of persons such as "arhats", and "whatever" is "the" "suchness" of "all" "dharmas" to be known as the ground, and whatever is "the" "suchness" of the "Jina" as the fruit, and whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the path such as the realization of emptiness—thus, "all" "these" "suchnesses" "have" "no" "distinctions" established individually whatsoever, but are of a single taste as the identity of the dharmadhātu. In this way, all things divided by dualistic dharmas such as existence and peace, past and future, and so forth, appear as distinct and are designated as such merely as conventions in the manner of appearance, but in the manner of abiding, the genuine reality, all dharmas are unarisen and unceasing, and by their very nature they become the equality of the nature of the dharmadhātu. Therefore, they cannot be differentiated by the three times, self and other, good and bad, and so forth. All abide as the nature of the dharmadhātu, the single bindu. Having realized this with wisdom endowed with a single instant, attaining complete and perfect awakening regarding all dharmas in the essence of the dharmakāya endowed with the supreme of all aspects of naturally occurring wisdom—this great awakening that is free from decrease and increase, unchanging and untransferring, is the ultimate fruit.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

translation: First, there is one stanza starting with "The awakening of the Sugatas": Thus, if "any" "bodhisattva" "desires" "to" "attain" "this" ultimate fruit to be attained, "the" "awakening" "of" "the" "Sugatas", which has the character of space and "is" "freed" "from" "distinct" "dharmas" such as that which is to be realized and that which realizes, and which possesses the nature of the body of non-dual naturally occurring wisdom or the body of dharmatā, they must apply or exert themselves in the "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom" that realizes the suchness of all dharmas, by means of "possessing" "methods" such as faith that seeks perfect awakening. Without "this" perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the "Victorious" "Guides", they "will" "not" ever "attain" that great awakening to be attained, because the cause of that ultimate fruit is definitively this very non-conceptual wisdom, the supreme of all paths, which bears the name of the perfection of wisdom.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Sentient beings": If one asks what is the reason that this profound dharma is difficult to realize by most: In this way, because they have been habituated to the mind clinging to entities since beginningless time, "sentient" "beings" "delight" "in" the "domain" of craving, the manner of self-grasping and so forth, "and" "desire" the apprehended "objects". They "abide" "in" the mind that "grasps" them, "and" because they thus fall into the domain of the fabrications of the grasped and the grasping, they are "unwise" regarding the meaning of suchness that is distinguished by the absence of grasped and grasping, and, not knowing how to engage their intellect in its manner, they become "foolish" and "deluded", just "like" abiding in the midst of "darkness". As for the meaning of the Mother, the "dharma" that is to be taught and "to" "be" "attained", it is "without" any object "to" "abide" in through apprehension, and is "without" "grasping" at anything whatsoever. Thus, those supramundane dharmas are not in harmony with the entire world and are especially exalted, and "therefore", "dispute" "arises" "with" "the" "worlds". This is because worldly beings grasp entities as existing, while the other teaches them to be non-existent. Therefore, worldly beings dispute, not having seen the manner of the dharma that teaches non-entities, but since the Tathāgata sees the nature of entities exactly as it is, he engages in conventions in harmony with the world, according to how those illusion-like dharmas—which, though lacking a nature, appear to the perspective of worldly beings—appear in the world. For that reason, it is said in other sūtras: "The worldly beings dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world. Whatever the world asserts to exist, I also assert to exist," and so forth.

translation: Second, there is one stanza starting with "Of the Jinas": What is the meaning that resembles the example just explained? Even if "these" "five" "perfections" such as generosity, which are the path "of" "the" "Jinas", "are accomplished" with perseverance for "many" "koṭis" and "niyutas" of "eons", "and" even if one "constantly" "relies" in this "world" upon "limitless", "vast" "aspiration prayers" that repeatedly engage in the vast path and fruit, that alone does not amount to a complete cause for attaining great awakening. The unerring cause of great awakening is the "immeasurable" skill in "means" of the Great Vehicle, such as dedicating the roots of virtue to omniscience, and the "wisdom" that realizes all dharmas as equality. If these two, means and wisdom, which are like the pair of wings for a bird flying in the sky, "are" "not" "separated", [one will attain great awakening]. If someone lacks such means and is separated from the wisdom that realizes suchness, they "will fall" "into" "the very" fruit "of the śrāvakas". Just as, for example, if a bird has a large body but lacks wings and leaps, it will fall downwards. If one possesses the perfection of wisdom of the ultimate abiding nature, means and wisdom are inseparable within the essence of that pristine wisdom, because it is the subject possessing the inseparability of the two truths.

translation: Second, there is one stanza starting with "The vehicle of the Buddha": Thus, "whoever" "desires" to "definitively" "emerge", meaning to reach, the state of great awakening by relying "upon" "this" unsurpassable "vehicle" "of" "the" "Buddha", the perfection of wisdom, which is the path of the single journey that is the cause of the ultimate great awakening—if it is asked what manner they should possess when entering it? Because they themselves have attained irreversible confidence in the teacher of this path, they "do" "not" "rely" "upon" "other" non-Buddhist "ascetics" "and" "brahmins" with the perception that they are showers of the path, and they do not place their trust deep down in the various paths taught by them. Having confidence in the meaning of the profound Dharma, they "single-pointedly" "delight" "in" "the" "holy" "Dharma", "and" without making much of other activities, they make the Dharma alone their priority. Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཉིས་པ། རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་དཔེ་དེ་ཡི་ཚུལ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་དོན་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ༷་བ༷་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱི༷་ལམ་དུ་གྱུར་པ་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ༷་ལྔ༷་པོ་འདི༷་ཡང༷་། དུས་བསྐལ་པ༷་བྱེ༷་བ༷་ཁྲག༷་ཁྲིག༷་མང༷་པོར༷་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་བསྒྲུབ༷་པར་བྱས༷་ཤིང༷་། ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་ཡང་ནས་ཡང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་སྨོན༷་ལམ༷་མཐའ༷་ཡས༷་པ་རྒྱ༷་ཆེན༷་པོ་འཇིག༷་རྟེན༷་འདི་ན་རྟག༷་ཏུ་བརྟེན༷་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང༷་དེ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཚང་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་རྒྱུ་མ་ནོར་བ་ནི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་རྣམས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དུ་བསྔོ་བ་སོགས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཐབས༷་མཁས་ཚད་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀུན་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་སྟེ་བྱ་མཁའ་ལ་འགྲོ་བའི་སྒྲོ་གཤོག་ཟུང་ལྟ་བུ་ཐབས་ཤེས་འདི་གཉིས་ཡ་མ་བྲལ༷་བ༷་ཡིན་ན། གང་ཞིག་ཐབས་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མེད་པ་དང་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་བྲལ་བ་ནི་ཉན༷་ཐོས༷་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཉི༷ད་དུ༷་ལྷུང༷་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན་བྱ་ལུས་ཆེ་ཡང་སྒྲོ་གཤོག་མེད་པར་དེ་མཆོངས་ན་འོག་ཏུ་ལྷུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །གནས་ལུགས་མཐར་ཐུག་པའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དང་ལྡན་ན་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའི་ངོ་བོར་ཐབས་ཤེས་འདུ་འབྲལ་མེད་དེ་བདེན་གཉིས་དབྱེར་མེད་པའི་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Second, there is one stanza starting with "Of the Jinas": What is the meaning that resembles the example just explained? Even if "these" "five" "perfections" such as generosity, which are the path "of" "the" "Jinas", "are accomplished" with perseverance for "many" "koṭis" and "niyutas" of "eons", "and" even if one "constantly" "relies" in this "world" upon "limitless", "vast" "aspiration prayers" that repeatedly engage in the vast path and fruit, that alone does not amount to a complete cause for attaining great awakening. The unerring cause of great awakening is the "immeasurable" skill in "means" of the Great Vehicle, such as dedicating the roots of virtue to omniscience, and the "wisdom" that realizes all dharmas as equality. If these two, means and wisdom, which are like the pair of wings for a bird flying in the sky, "are" "not" "separated", [one will attain great awakening]. If someone lacks such means and is separated from the wisdom that realizes suchness, they "will fall" "into" "the very" fruit "of the śrāvakas". Just as, for example, if a bird has a large body but lacks wings and leaps, it will fall downwards. If one possesses the perfection of wisdom of the ultimate abiding nature, means and wisdom are inseparable within the essence of that pristine wisdom, because it is the subject possessing the inseparability of the two truths.

གཉིས་པ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཐེག་པ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། དེ་ལྟར་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་རྒྱུ་བགྲོད་པ་གཅིག་པུའི་ལམ་སངས༷་རྒྱས༷་ཀྱི་ཐེག༷་པ༷་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི༷་ལ༷་བརྟེན་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་གོ་འཕང་ལ་ངེས༷་པར༷་འབྱུང༷་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱིན་པར་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་གང༷་ཡིན་པ་དེས་ནི། ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པས་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་གཞན་དོན་ལ་དམིགས་པའི་སྙིང་རྗེའི་རྩ་བ་ཅན། ཐབས་ཀྱི་ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་ཅན། འབྲས་བུ་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་སྲིད་དུ་མཛད་པ་ཅན་ཡིན་པས་དེ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་ཚུལ་དང་ཞུགས་པའི་གང་ཟག་གི་ཚུལ་ནི། མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་འགྲོ༷་བ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ༷་རིས་སུ་མ་ཆད་པར་སེམ༷ས་སྙོམས༷་པར་བྱས་ཏེ་ཕ༷་དང་མའི༷་འདུ༷་ཤེས༷་དང༷་སྤུན་དང་སྲིང་མོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པ་དང་། གཏན་དུ་ཕན༷་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་དང༷་འཕྲལ༷་དུ་བདེ་བར་འདོད་པ་བྱམས༷་པའི༷་ཡི༷ད་ཀྱིས༷་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གི་དོན་ལ་བརྟུལ༷་བ་སྟེ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ༷་ཞིང༷་། ཁྲོ་བ་དང་རྣམ་པར་འཚེ་བའི་ཐ༷་བ༷་མེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་གཡོ་དང་རྒྱུ་མེད་པར་རྒྱུད་དྲང༷་ལ༷་ངག་གིས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་དང་མཐུན་པར་བརྗོད་པ་སོགས་ཚིག་འཇམ༷་པོར་སྨྲ༷་བར༷་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་པའི་ལུས་ཀྱི་ལས་སུའང་བྱ་སྟེ། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་ཟོལ་མེད་པར་ཕན་པའི་སེམས་སྐྱེད་པ་ཅན་དེས་དེ་དང་ཚུལ་མི་མཐུན་པ་གཡོ་སྒྱུ་དང་གནོད་སེམས་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Second, there is one stanza starting with "The vehicle of the Buddha": Thus, "whoever" "desires" to "definitively" "emerge", meaning to reach, the state of great awakening by relying "upon" "this" unsurpassable "vehicle" "of" "the" "Buddha", the perfection of wisdom, which is the path of the single journey that is the cause of the ultimate great awakening—if it is asked what manner they should possess when entering it? Since the Great Vehicle is rooted in compassion focused on the welfare of others, acts conjointly with means, and has as its fruit the performance of the welfare of sentient beings for as long as space remains, the manner of engaging in it and the manner of the person who has engaged is as follows: Generating an "equanimous" "mind", without bias, "towards" "all" limitless "beings", they abide in "the" "perception" "of" them as "parents", "and" the perception of them as brothers and sisters, and so forth. With "a" "mind" "of" ultimate "benefit" "and" "a" "mind" "of" "loving-kindness" desiring their temporary happiness, they "should" "endeavor", meaning strive, for the welfare of those sentient beings. "Having" "no" "malice" such as anger and violence, and having a "straightforward" continuum without deceit or guile, they should "speak" "gentle" words, such as teaching the Dharma with speech and speaking harmoniously, and they should also perform bodily actions of loving-kindness. Because, for one who has generated a mind of unfeigned benefit for sentient beings, it is impossible to act in a manner discordant with that, such as with deceit, guile, or malicious intent.

དང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་མགོན་ལ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། འཇིག༷་རྟེན༷་གསུམ་གྱི་མགོ༷ན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ༷་གན༷ས་བརྟན༷་རབ༷་འབྱོར༷་གྱིས་ཡོངས༷་སུ་ཞུ༷ས༷་པ༷། ཡོན༷་ཏན༷་རྒྱ༷་མཚོ༷་ཚད་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་གི་ཉོ༷ན་མོང༷ས་པ་མ༷་མཆིས༷་པའི་རྟག༷ས་དང་མཚན་མ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་བདག་ལ་བསྟན༷་དུ་གསོལ༷། དོན་གཉིས་སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཐུ༷་ཆེ༷་བ༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག༷་ཇི༷་ལྟར༷་ན་རྟགས་གང་གིས་མཚོན་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་སླར༷་ལྡོག༷་པར་མི༷་འགྱུར༷་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་ཤེས་པར་འགྱུར༷་བ༷་དེ༷་ལྟར༷་བྱང་སེམས་བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་གི་ཡོན༷་ཏན༷་ཚད་མེད་པ་ལས་ཕྱོགས༷་སམ་ཆ་ཤས་ཙམ༷་ཞིག་རྒྱལ༷་བས༷་བདག་ལ་ལུང༷་བསྟན༷་དུ་གསོལ༷་ཞེས་ཞུས་པའོ། །༈ལན་གྱིས་རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: "Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".
