གཙང༷་མར་བྱས༷་ཤིང་གཙང༷་མའི༷་གོས༷་འཆང༷་བ་སོགས་གདུལ་བྱའི་ཡིད་དང་འཐད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གཙང་བ་དང་། ལུས་ངག་ཡིད་ཀྱི་སྒོ་གསུམ༷་པོ༷་ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བས་དབེན༷་ཞིང༷་དྲི་མ་མེད་པའི་ཤེལ་ལྟར་དག༷་པ་དང་། འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་རང་མཚངས་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་མི་ཆགས་པར་སྦྱང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལེན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་རྙེད༷་པ་འདོ༷ད་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། སེར་སྣ་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་ནས་རང་རྒྱུད་ཡོན་ཏན་མཆོག་གིས་མཛེས་ཤིང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་བྱེད་པས་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཁྱུ༷་མཆོག༷་ཏུ་ངང་གིས་གྱུར་པ་དང་། དུས་རྟག༷་ཏུ༷་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་སྟེ་ཆོས་དང་རང་རྒྱུད་འདྲེས་པས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་ཞེས་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཉམས་འོག་ཏུ་ཚུད་པས་དེ་དང་བློ་ངང་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཅི་སྨྲ་ཅི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་མ་འདས་པར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་ཆགས་ལྡན་པ་དག་གིས་སྤྱོད་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་བཟོད་པའི་དད་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པས་ན་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པས་ལམ་གཞན་སྟོན་པ་དང་དམྱལ་བ་སོགས་མངོན་དུ་སྤྲུལ་ནས་འཁོར་བ་ལ་ཡིད་སྐྲག་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་བཟློག་སྟེ་ལམ་གཟུགས་བརྙན་བསྟན་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་བདུད་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན། བདུ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་ཡུ༷ལ་ལ༷ས་འདས༷་ཤིང༷་གཞན༷་གྱི༷་དྲིང༷་ལ༷་མི༷་འཇོག༷་པ་སྟེ་གཞན་ལ་རག་མ་ལས་པའི་རང་གི་བློ་སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། བས༷མ་གཏན༷་བཞི༷་ལ༷་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའམ་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དེར༷་རོ་མྱོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི༷་གན༷ས་པ་དང་། དངོས་པོ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པ་དང་གྲགས༷་པ༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་དུལ་བས་ཁྲོ༷་བས༷་སེམ༷ས་འཁྲུགས་པའམ་ཀུན་ནས་དཀྲིས༷་པ་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་།

"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཙང༷་མར་བྱས༷་ཤིང་གཙང༷་མའི༷་གོས༷་འཆང༷་བ་སོགས་གདུལ་བྱའི་ཡིད་དང་འཐད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གཙང་བ་དང་། ལུས་ངག་ཡིད་ཀྱི་སྒོ་གསུམ༷་པོ༷་ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བས་དབེན༷་ཞིང༷་དྲི་མ་མེད་པའི་ཤེལ་ལྟར་དག༷་པ་དང་། འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་རང་མཚངས་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་མི་ཆགས་པར་སྦྱང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལེན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་རྙེད༷་པ་འདོ༷ད་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། སེར་སྣ་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་ནས་རང་རྒྱུད་ཡོན་ཏན་མཆོག་གིས་མཛེས་ཤིང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་བྱེད་པས་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཁྱུ༷་མཆོག༷་ཏུ་ངང་གིས་གྱུར་པ་དང་། དུས་རྟག༷་ཏུ༷་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་སྟེ་ཆོས་དང་རང་རྒྱུད་འདྲེས་པས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་ཞེས་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཉམས་འོག་ཏུ་ཚུད་པས་དེ་དང་བློ་ངང་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཅི་སྨྲ་ཅི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་མ་འདས་པར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་ཆགས་ལྡན་པ་དག་གིས་སྤྱོད་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་བཟོད་པའི་དད་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པས་ན་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པས་ལམ་གཞན་སྟོན་པ་དང་དམྱལ་བ་སོགས་མངོན་དུ་སྤྲུལ་ནས་འཁོར་བ་ལ་ཡིད་སྐྲག་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་བཟློག་སྟེ་ལམ་གཟུགས་བརྙན་བསྟན་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་བདུད་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན། བདུ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་ཡུ༷ལ་ལ༷ས་འདས༷་ཤིང༷་གཞན༷་གྱི༷་དྲིང༷་ལ༷་མི༷་འཇོག༷་པ་སྟེ་གཞན་ལ་རག་མ་ལས་པའི་རང་གི་བློ་སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། བས༷མ་གཏན༷་བཞི༷་ལ༷་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའམ་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དེར༷་རོ་མྱོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི༷་གན༷ས་པ་དང་། དངོས་པོ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པ་དང་གྲགས༷་པ༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་དུལ་བས་ཁྲོ༷་བས༷་སེམ༷ས་འཁྲུགས་པའམ་ཀུན་ནས་དཀྲིས༷་པ་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་།
[1-255] translation already produced for this document:
"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

[1-256] source:
རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

Not being attached to desires themselves and being skillful in means, "even" "if" they "become" "householders" for the sake of others, they "constantly" let go of "all" "entities" "without" "attachment". Being influenced by the realization of selflessness and a compassionate mind for others, they abandon all wrong livelihoods and extreme actions that arise from holding their own benefit as paramount. Moreover, how is this? "For" "the" "sake" "of" their "own" "livelihood", they "do" "not" "seek" "wealth" through means that are "light" in their ripening results, such as killing or flattery. They "do" "not" "perform" "spells" of destructive magic involving "fierce" "actions" that harm others for their own sake. They "are" "not" ones who perform "spells" that subjugate "women" or bring them under their control through the power of attachment. In order to proclaim themselves, they "do" "not" verbally "prophesy" regarding "embodied" beings "of" "the" "desire" realm who are residing in the womb or are about to be born, saying, "This" "will" "be" a "boy" "or" a "girl". As indicated by these, they possess the signs of completely pure livelihood and extremes of action. By being "completely" "isolated" from various distractions that delight in the activities of the three doors—namely action, speech, and proliferation—they "endeavor" "in" "the" "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom". Since their mindstreams have become peaceful, wherever they reside, they are "free" from mutual "strife" "and" "disputes" and so forth, "and" their "mind" "of" "loving-kindness", which cannot be taken away by circumstances, is "extremely" "stable".

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་དེའི་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་ཕྱིར་ལྡོག་པ།**
translation: In the second, there are three: the profound conduct of the ultimate subject, the vast conduct of the relative subject, and the conduct of skillful means that unifies them.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཙང༷་མར་བྱས༷་ཤིང་གཙང༷་མའི༷་གོས༷་འཆང༷་བ་སོགས་གདུལ་བྱའི་ཡིད་དང་འཐད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གཙང་བ་དང་། ལུས་ངག་ཡིད་ཀྱི་སྒོ་གསུམ༷་པོ༷་ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བས་དབེན༷་ཞིང༷་དྲི་མ་མེད་པའི་ཤེལ་ལྟར་དག༷་པ་དང་། འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་རང་མཚངས་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་མི་ཆགས་པར་སྦྱང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལེན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་རྙེད༷་པ་འདོ༷ད་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། སེར་སྣ་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་ནས་རང་རྒྱུད་ཡོན་ཏན་མཆོག་གིས་མཛེས་ཤིང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་བྱེད་པས་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཁྱུ༷་མཆོག༷་ཏུ་ངང་གིས་གྱུར་པ་དང་། དུས་རྟག༷་ཏུ༷་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་སྟེ་ཆོས་དང་རང་རྒྱུད་འདྲེས་པས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་ཞེས་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཉམས་འོག་ཏུ་ཚུད་པས་དེ་དང་བློ་ངང་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཅི་སྨྲ་ཅི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་མ་འདས་པར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་ཆགས་ལྡན་པ་དག་གིས་སྤྱོད་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་བཟོད་པའི་དད་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པས་ན་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པས་ལམ་གཞན་སྟོན་པ་དང་དམྱལ་བ་སོགས་མངོན་དུ་སྤྲུལ་ནས་འཁོར་བ་ལ་ཡིད་སྐྲག་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་བཟློག་སྟེ་ལམ་གཟུགས་བརྙན་བསྟན་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་བདུད་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན། བདུ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་ཡུ༷ལ་ལ༷ས་འདས༷་ཤིང༷་གཞན༷་གྱི༷་དྲིང༷་ལ༷་མི༷་འཇོག༷་པ་སྟེ་གཞན་ལ་རག་མ་ལས་པའི་རང་གི་བློ་སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། བས༷མ་གཏན༷་བཞི༷་ལ༷་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའམ་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དེར༷་རོ་མྱོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི༷་གན༷ས་པ་དང་། དངོས་པོ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པ་དང་གྲགས༷་པ༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་དུལ་བས་ཁྲོ༷་བས༷་སེམ༷ས་འཁྲུགས་པའམ་ཀུན་ནས་དཀྲིས༷་པ་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་།
[1-255] translation already produced for this document:
"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

[1-256] source:
རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

Not being attached to desires themselves and being skillful in means, "even" "if" they "become" "householders" for the sake of others, they "constantly" let go of "all" "entities" "without" "attachment". Being influenced by the realization of selflessness and a compassionate mind for others, they abandon all wrong livelihoods and extreme actions that arise from holding their own benefit as paramount. Moreover, how is this? "For" "the" "sake" "of" their "own" "livelihood", they "do" "not" "seek" "wealth" through means that are "light" in their ripening results, such as killing or flattery. They "do" "not" "perform" "spells" of destructive magic involving "fierce" "actions" that harm others for their own sake. They "are" "not" ones who perform "spells" that subjugate "women" or bring them under their control through the power of attachment. In order to proclaim themselves, they "do" "not" verbally "prophesy" regarding "embodied" beings "of" "the" "desire" realm who are residing in the womb or are about to be born, saying, "This" "will" "be" a "boy" "or" a "girl". As indicated by these, they possess the signs of completely pure livelihood and extremes of action. By being "completely" "isolated" from various distractions that delight in the activities of the three doors—namely action, speech, and proliferation—they "endeavor" "in" "the" "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom". Since their mindstreams have become peaceful, wherever they reside, they are "free" from mutual "strife" "and" "disputes" and so forth, "and" their "mind" "of" "loving-kindness", which cannot be taken away by circumstances, is "extremely" "stable".

heading: **དོན་དམ་པའི་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཟབ་མོའི་སྤྱོད་པ།**
translation: The profound conduct of the ultimate subject. In the first, there are two: recognizing the profound meaning that is to be practiced, and how to practice it.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

heading: **ཟབ་མོ་ཉིད་བཤད་པ།**
translation: The first. Form, feeling, and so forth is one verse. "Form", "and" "feeling", "and" "perception", "formation", "and" "consciousness"—that is, phenomena—are "profound". If one asks how they are profound, they are empty because they are isolated from an intrinsic "nature"; they are "without" "marks" such as being suitable as form, "and" because the wishing of fixating on them is "completely" "peaceful", they cannot be apprehended by the intellect. So, "for" "example", "like" "searching" to "reach" the "depth" "of" "the" "ocean" "with" "an" "arrow", one does not find anything and say, "It is like this." Likewise, "if" one has "examined" and investigated "by" means of the "wisdom" that analyzes reality itself, one "does" "not" "find" the "depth" "of" "the" "aggregates".

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཙང༷་མར་བྱས༷་ཤིང་གཙང༷་མའི༷་གོས༷་འཆང༷་བ་སོགས་གདུལ་བྱའི་ཡིད་དང་འཐད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གཙང་བ་དང་། ལུས་ངག་ཡིད་ཀྱི་སྒོ་གསུམ༷་པོ༷་ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བས་དབེན༷་ཞིང༷་དྲི་མ་མེད་པའི་ཤེལ་ལྟར་དག༷་པ་དང་། འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་རང་མཚངས་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་མི་ཆགས་པར་སྦྱང་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལེན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་རྙེད༷་པ་འདོ༷ད་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། སེར་སྣ་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་ནས་རང་རྒྱུད་ཡོན་ཏན་མཆོག་གིས་མཛེས་ཤིང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་བྱེད་པས་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཁྱུ༷་མཆོག༷་ཏུ་ངང་གིས་གྱུར་པ་དང་། དུས་རྟག༷་ཏུ༷་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་སྟེ་ཆོས་དང་རང་རྒྱུད་འདྲེས་པས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་ཞེས་ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཉམས་འོག་ཏུ་ཚུད་པས་དེ་དང་བློ་ངང་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཅི་སྨྲ་ཅི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་མ་འདས་པར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་ཆགས་ལྡན་པ་དག་གིས་སྤྱོད་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྲོ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་བཟོད་པའི་དད་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པས་ན་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པས་ལམ་གཞན་སྟོན་པ་དང་དམྱལ་བ་སོགས་མངོན་དུ་སྤྲུལ་ནས་འཁོར་བ་ལ་ཡིད་སྐྲག་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་བཟློག་སྟེ་ལམ་གཟུགས་བརྙན་བསྟན་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་བདུད་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན། བདུ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་ཡུ༷ལ་ལ༷ས་འདས༷་ཤིང༷་གཞན༷་གྱི༷་དྲིང༷་ལ༷་མི༷་འཇོག༷་པ་སྟེ་གཞན་ལ་རག་མ་ལས་པའི་རང་གི་བློ་སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། བས༷མ་གཏན༷་བཞི༷་ལ༷་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའམ་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་དེར༷་རོ་མྱོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི༷་གན༷ས་པ་དང་། དངོས་པོ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པ་དང་གྲགས༷་པ༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་པ་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་དུལ་བས་ཁྲོ༷་བས༷་སེམ༷ས་འཁྲུགས་པའམ་ཀུན་ནས་དཀྲིས༷་པ་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་།
[1-255] translation already produced for this document:
"Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

[1-256] source:
རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

Not being attached to desires themselves and being skillful in means, "even" "if" they "become" "householders" for the sake of others, they "constantly" let go of "all" "entities" "without" "attachment". Being influenced by the realization of selflessness and a compassionate mind for others, they abandon all wrong livelihoods and extreme actions that arise from holding their own benefit as paramount. Moreover, how is this? "For" "the" "sake" "of" their "own" "livelihood", they "do" "not" "seek" "wealth" through means that are "light" in their ripening results, such as killing or flattery. They "do" "not" "perform" "spells" of destructive magic involving "fierce" "actions" that harm others for their own sake. They "are" "not" ones who perform "spells" that subjugate "women" or bring them under their control through the power of attachment. In order to proclaim themselves, they "do" "not" verbally "prophesy" regarding "embodied" beings "of" "the" "desire" realm who are residing in the womb or are about to be born, saying, "This" "will" "be" a "boy" "or" a "girl". As indicated by these, they possess the signs of completely pure livelihood and extremes of action. By being "completely" "isolated" from various distractions that delight in the activities of the three doors—namely action, speech, and proliferation—they "endeavor" "in" "the" "supreme" "perfection" "of" "wisdom". Since their mindstreams have become peaceful, wherever they reside, they are "free" from mutual "strife" "and" "disputes" and so forth, "and" their "mind" "of" "loving-kindness", which cannot be taken away by circumstances, is "extremely" "stable".

heading: **དེ་ལ་སྤྱད་པས་བསོད་ནམས་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱ་བ།**
translation: In the second, there are two: the actual subject and abandoning objections to it.

Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). "Making" things "clean" and "wearing" "clean" "clothes" and so forth, they engage in clean behavior that agrees with the minds of those to be tamed. "The" "three" avenues of body, speech, and mind are "isolated" from misdeeds "and" "pure" like a flawless crystal. Seeing the intrinsic flaws of conditioned phenomena, they are not overly attached to them, and by adopting ascetic qualities and the like, they "do" "not" "desire" "gain". Having outshone the discordant factors of the perfections such as stinginess, their mindstreams are beautified by supreme qualities, and since they make the benefit of others their main priority, they naturally become the "best" of beings. "Constantly" "desiring" the profound "Dharma"—meaning that since the Dharma and their own mindstream have blended, at all times they proceed endowed with dharmatā—because they have brought the profound dharmatā into their experience, their mind naturally does not separate from it, and whatever they say or do accords with it and does not transcend it, just as, for example, all the behavior of passionate beings proceeds endowed with passion. Because they have attained receptive faith in the profound Dharma, even if demonic emanations of the Evil One teach another path or manifest hells and so forth to frighten their minds about saṃsāra, trying by various means to turn them away from the Mahāyāna path by showing a facsimile path, they recognize them as māras; therefore, because they are unharmed by the various activities of māras, they "have" "passed" "beyond" "the" "domain" "of" "māra" "and" "do" "not" "depend" "on" "others", meaning they possess their own mental strength that is not reliant on others. Although they meditate on or attain meditative equipoise "in" "the" "four" "dhyānas", they "do" "not" "abide" "in" "that" "dhyāna" by savoring its taste and so forth. Because they know phenomena to be like an illusion, they themselves "do" "not" "desire" fame and "renown", and because their mindstreams are tamed by the holy Dharma, their "minds" are "not" disturbed or completely entangled "by" "anger".

རང་ཉིད་འདོད་པ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་ཤིང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ༷་པར༷་གྱུར༷་ཀྱང༷་རྟ༷ག་ཏུ༷་དངོས༷་པོ༷་ཀུན༷་ལ་མ༷་ཆགས༷་པར་གཏོང་བ་དང་། བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པ་དང་གཞན་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་སོང་བས་རང་གི་དོན་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤང་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རང་འཚོ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷་ནི༷་སྲོག་གཅོད་པ་དང་ཁ་གསག་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམ་སྨིན་ཡ༷ངས༷་ཏེ་ཡང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལོངས༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་ཚོལ༷་བར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། རང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་གཞན་ལ་གནོད་པ་དྲག༷་ཤུལ༷་སྤྱོ༷ད་པའི་སྔ༷གས་མངོན་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ལས་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བུ༷ད་མེ༷ད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར༷་བའི་སྔ༷གས་བྱེད་པ་མིན༷་པ་དང་། རང་ཉིད་བསྒྲགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདོ༷ད་པའི༷་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ལ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་མངལ་ན་གནས་པའམ་གདོད་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལ་འདི་ནི་ཕོ༷འམ་མོར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ༷་ཞེས་ངག་གིས་ལུང་སྟོན༷་པར་མི༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་ནས་ལོག་པའི་འཚོ་བ་དང་། ལོག་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟགས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་གསུམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ལས་དང་སྨྲ་བ་དང་སྤྲོས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གཡེངས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་རོལ༷་ཏུ་ཕྱིན༷་པ་མཆོག༷་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ་དང་། རྒྱུད་དེས་པར་གྱུར་པས་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེང་ཕན་ཚུན་འཐབ༷་པ་དང༷་རྩོད༷་པ་སོགས་དང༷་བྲལ༷་ཞིང༷་བྱམ༷ས་པའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རྐྱེན་གྱིས་མི་འཕྲོག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟན༷་པ་དང་།

translation: The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

Whatever has been briefly indicated and "explained" "by" the transcendent and accomplished conquerors, the "buddhas", "and" its meaning has been indicated "and" "thoroughly" "applied" extensively, and whatever "Dharma" has been "thoroughly" "taught" along with justified reasoning that proves it—"all" "this" that has been spoken, although in reality all expressions and things expressed are unapprehendable and inexpressible, "knowing" that it "exhausts" "merely" in names of "expression" conventionally, "even" "if" one were to indicate measureless doors of Dharma and "express" them in the manner of refuting or proving for "many" "ten millions" of "hundred billions" of "eons", though the words of expression would not be exhausted, by that there is "no" "exhaustion" of faults "and" "no" "increase" of qualities whatsoever "as for" the essence of the "Dharmadhātu"—it remains eternally as equality, inexpressible, and free from decrease or increase. The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

translation: The first. "The core of grains or oil" and so forth is one verse. Thus, if one says: "Even in terms of conventional designations, the mind that attains awakening is momentary and cannot be accumulated; therefore, how does that mind attain awakening, free from obscurations? Because the former mind alone does not abandon obscurations, and the latter alone, not depending on the former, does not abandon them either, and the two are not accumulated together." First, to use an example well known in the world: just as when the two, the "core" "of" oil such as "grains" and so forth, which is liquid oil, and the "flame" of a lamp "burning" "meet", it is "not" "burned" up completely "by" that "first" momentary flame alone, "nor" is "it" "burned" "without" "that" first one; and the "core" of the oil is "not" "burned" by the "last" "meeting" of the liquid oil and the "flame" alone, "nor" is the "core" "burned" "without" the "last" "flame"; nevertheless, when the continuum of moments from the first momentary flame to the last is complete, the core of the oil or butter is all burned by the fire and completely exhausted—this exists. One should understand this by using it as an example.

The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

Whatever has been briefly indicated and "explained" "by" the transcendent and accomplished conquerors, the "buddhas", "and" its meaning has been indicated "and" "thoroughly" "applied" extensively, and whatever "Dharma" has been "thoroughly" "taught" along with justified reasoning that proves it—"all" "this" that has been spoken, although in reality all expressions and things expressed are unapprehendable and inexpressible, "knowing" that it "exhausts" "merely" in names of "expression" conventionally, "even" "if" one were to indicate measureless doors of Dharma and "express" them in the manner of refuting or proving for "many" "ten millions" of "hundred billions" of "eons", though the words of expression would not be exhausted, by that there is "no" "exhaustion" of faults "and" "no" "increase" of qualities whatsoever "as for" the essence of the "Dharmadhātu"—it remains eternally as equality, inexpressible, and free from decrease or increase. The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

heading: **མི་འཐད་པ་མེད་ཚུལ།**
translation: The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. "Likewise" here on the occasion of investigating the fruit of the path, "even" the initially generated mind, or the "first" "mind", "is" the "cause" of "awakening", and it is "not" the case that "that" mind "ceases" "and" its indirect fruit, "awakening", is "nonexistent"; by way of infallible cause and effect, the attainment of the fruit, awakening, from the causes, the prior and subsequent minds of the stages of the path, exists infallibly.

The fourth. "That merit, too" and so forth is one verse. Thus, although conventionally there is immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable merit in considering and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so forth, ultimately, even merit has no nature. Thus, thoroughly "knowing" that "that" "merit", "too", arising from explaining and so forth, is "vain" because it is not established as its own characteristic, "and" "likewise" is "emptiness" because it is empty of aspects such as suffering, "and" is "hollow" because it is signless, "and" is "insubstantial" because it arises dependently without being established by its own essence, "and" is "coreless" because it is devoid of anything to be apprehended by objectification; "if" one "thus" "courses" in the "course" on the "perfection" of "wisdom" "of" the "sugatas", at the "time" of coursing in such a course, one "fully" "grasps" "unfathomable" "merit". Here, it is also explained that because it lacks its own characteristic, it is vain; and emptiness and the other two are emptiness. By reason of the three beginning with the emptiness of emptiness, it is vain. By reason of the five beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned, it is hollow. By reason of the emptiness of nature and so forth, it is coreless. In reality, regarding the way entities are natureless, from the perspective of conceptual isolation, because it is accumulated from many things and lacks firmness like something spongy, it is vain; because it is like an artificial reflection such as a lion and so forth, it is hollow; and because it cannot stand on its own but depends on others, being fickle and unreliable, it is insubstantial—thus it is taught by way of synonyms for false words.

translation: The second. "Having found a seed" and so forth is one verse. Thus, the way of dependent origination is as follows. "Having found", that is, having come to possess, a "seed" itself that is endowed with the collection suitable to generate its own fruit, its fruit, various "grains" "and" "rice" and "so forth", "will arise", and "the" "fruit" "of" "that" seed is "not" "existent" in "that" seed from the beginning, nor is it "nonexistent" in the manner of being suitable to arise, because whatever exists previously does not need a cause, and if it were nonexistent in the manner of being suitable to arise, the meaning of "cause" would become nonexistent. If it is like that, when its nature is investigated, although it is free from the nature of an entity such as existent or nonexistent, arising infallibly as an appearance in the manner of an illusion and so forth is the way of the dharma of dependent origination. In that manner, "this" "awakening" "of" the "Victorious Ones" "also" "will" "arise" by the power of dependent origination; when investigated, it is "free" from the "nature" of a truly established "entity", "so" one should know that it "will" "arise" "like" an "illusion".

The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. "Likewise" here on the occasion of investigating the fruit of the path, "even" the initially generated mind, or the "first" "mind", "is" the "cause" of "awakening", and it is "not" the case that "that" mind "ceases" "and" its indirect fruit, "awakening", is "nonexistent"; by way of infallible cause and effect, the attainment of the fruit, awakening, from the causes, the prior and subsequent minds of the stages of the path, exists infallibly.

heading: **ཡོན་ཏན་རྫོགས་པ་འཐད་པ།**
translation: The second is the justification for the completion of qualities. "By drops of water" and so forth is one verse. If one asks: "Since entities are momentary and cannot be accumulated, even if one habituates for countless eons, it is impossible for them to gather together and increase, so how does one attain the fruit of awakening where all qualities are complete and perfected?" Although all entities are momentary, because each subsequent mind becomes distinguished in qualities in dependence upon each preceding mind, there is ultimately a complete perfection of qualities. Thus, when a "pot" is filled "by" accumulating "drops" "of" "water" from one to many, just "as" accumulating "gradually", "little" by "little", from the "first" drop to the "last", finally "fills" "that" pot "completely", thus, the attainment of buddhahood in dependence on completing the number of mind-generations gradually over the ten grounds and five paths is "likewise" according to that example: "even" the "first" "mind" generated during the stage of earnest conduct is the "cause" of "supreme" "awakening", and although qualities are not completely perfected by that alone, one "will" attain "buddhahood" through the door of "perfecting" "white" "qualities" "gradually" higher and higher, just as a pot is not filled completely by one drop of water but is filled by many. By means of filling with many instead of filling with one, it becomes the example for attaining buddhahood through the completion of many moments of mind generation; and although the entity of water is momentary, just as the pot is filled by the mutual gathering of the continuum of drops, one should understand that each subsequent moment becoming distinguished from the preceding by the continuum of momentary minds is also in that manner.

The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. "Likewise" here on the occasion of investigating the fruit of the path, "even" the initially generated mind, or the "first" "mind", "is" the "cause" of "awakening", and it is "not" the case that "that" mind "ceases" "and" its indirect fruit, "awakening", is "nonexistent"; by way of infallible cause and effect, the attainment of the fruit, awakening, from the causes, the prior and subsequent minds of the stages of the path, exists infallibly.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[1-276] source:
དང་པོ་ལ། དཔེ་དོན་གཉིས་ཀྱི།
[1-276] translation already produced for this document:
The first. In this, there are two: the example and the meaning.

[1-277] source:
དང་པོ། འབྲུ་མར་སྙིང་པོ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ན་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་ནི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཡིན་ལ་དེ་བསག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་དེས་སྒྲིབ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཐོབ་སྟེ་སེམས་སྔ་མ་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་སྒྲིབ་པ་མི་སྤོང་ལ། སྔ་མ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པའི་ཕྱི་མ་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་མི་སྤོང་ཞིང་དེ་གཉིས་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་བསགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། ཐོག་མར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་གྲགས་པའི་དཔེར་བྱ་ན། ཇི་ལྟར་འབྲུ༷་ལ་སོགས་པའི་མར༷་གྱི་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་སྟེ་ཞུན་མར་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དང་མར་མེའི་མེ་ལྕེ་འབར༷་བ༷་གཉིས་ཕྲ༷ད་པ༷་ན། མེ་ལྕེ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིས༷་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང་པོ་དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་དེ༷་མི༷་ཚིག༷་པ་དང་། མར་ཁུ་དང་མེ༷་ལྕེ༷་ཕྲ༷ད་པ༷་ཐ༷་མ༷་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་མར་གྱི་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ༷་མེ༷་ལྕེ༷་ཐ༷་མ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་མོད་ཀྱི། མེ་ལྕེ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང་པོ་ནས་ཐ་མའི་བར་གྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་གི་རྒྱུན་རྫོགས་པ་ན་འབྲུ་མར་གྱི་སྙིང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེས་ཚིག་པར་བྱས་ནས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་དཔེར་བྱས་ནས་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
[1-277] translation already produced for this document:
The first. "The core of grains or oil" and so forth is one verse. Thus, if one says: "Even in terms of conventional designations, the mind that attains awakening is momentary and cannot be accumulated; therefore, how does that mind attain awakening, free from obscurations? Because the former mind alone does not abandon obscurations, and the latter alone, not depending on the former, does not abandon them either, and the two are not accumulated together." First, to use an example well known in the world: just as when the two, the "core" "of" oil such as "grains" and so forth, which is liquid oil, and the "flame" of a lamp "burning" "meet", it is "not" "burned" up completely "by" that "first" momentary flame alone, "nor" is "it" "burned" "without" "that" first one; and the "core" of the oil is "not" "burned" by the "last" "meeting" of the liquid oil and the "flame" alone, "nor" is the "core" "burned" "without" the "last" "flame"; nevertheless, when the continuum of moments from the first momentary flame to the last is complete, the core of the oil or butter is all burned by the fire and completely exhausted—this exists. One should understand this by using it as an example.

[1-278] source:
གཉིས་པ་དང་པོའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་མ་ཐག་པ་དང༷་པོའི༷་སེམ༷ས་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཙམ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས༷་སྤང་བྱ་མཐའ་དག་དང་བྲལ་བའི་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མཆོག༷་ལ་རེག༷་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ལ༷། དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ༷་ལ༷་རེག༷་པར༷་ནུས༷་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཞིང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་ཁ་མ་རྒྱུན་གྱི་ཐ༷་མའི༷་སེམ༷ས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་གཅིག་པུ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས༷་ཀྱང་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཆེན་པོ་དྲི་མ་མཐའ་དག་ཞི༷་བ༷་ཐོབ༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ༷། དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ༷་ཐོབ༷་པར་ནུས༷་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་མོད་ཀྱི་སྔ་མ་སྔ་མ་ལས་ཕྱི་མ་ཕྱི་མ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་གྱིས་མཐར་སྤང་བྱ་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པ་ནི་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བསྙོན་དུ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ༷། །
[1-278] translation already produced for this document:
The second. "Even the first mind" and so forth is one verse. Like the example just explained, the "supreme" "awakening" free from all that is to be abandoned is "not" "touched" "by" the "first" "mind" just after generation alone; "nor" "can" "that" awakening be "touched" "without" "it"; and the great "awakening" where all stains are "pacified" is "not" "attained" "by" the "last" "mind" of the continuum on the verge of attaining awakening alone either, "nor" "can" "that" awakening be "attained" "without" "it"; nevertheless, the attainment of the great awakening where all that is to be abandoned has finally been abandoned by the continuum of mind where each subsequent moment has become more distinguished than the preceding is the nature of dependent origination, undeniable.

[1-279] source:
གཉིས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐོབ་ཚུལ་ལ། ཡོན་ཏན་ཐོབ་པ་འཐད་པ་དང་། ཡོན་ཏན་རྫོགས་པ་འཐད་པ་གཉིས།
[1-279] translation already produced for this document:
The second is the way of attaining qualities. In this, there are two: the justification for attaining qualities, and the justification for the completion of qualities.

[1-280] source:
དང་པོ་ལ། མི་འཐད་པ་མེད་ཚུལ་དང་། རྟེན་བྲེལ་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ངེས་པར་འཐད་པ་བཤད་པ་གཉིས།
[1-280] translation already produced for this document:
The first. In this, there are two: the way it is not unjustified, and explaining how it is definitely justified by way of dependent origination.

[1-281] source:
དང་པོ། ས་བོན་ལས་ནི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། གང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སེམས་དང་པོ་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་དུ་སྡོད་ན་རྟག་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། མི་སྡོད་པར་འགག་ན་སྐད་ཅིག་མའི་སེམས་དེ་སྙེད་པ་རེ་རེ་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འབྱུང་བ་མེད་པས་བསྐལ་པ་དུ་མར་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་འབྱུང་བ་འདི་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མི་འཐད་དོ་ཞེས་རྒོལ་བ་ལ་ལན་བསྟན་པ་ནི། འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་རྒྱུ་ཡི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་རྣམས་སྔོན་དུ་སོང་བ་ན་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་བཤོལ་དུ་མེད་པ་ནི་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ས༷་བོན༷་ལ༷ས་ནི༷་མྱུ༷་གུ༷་དང་དེ་ལས་སྡོང་བུ་མེ༷་ཏོག༷་དང་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་རྣམ༷ས་རིམ་པར་འབྱུང༷་བ་ཡོད་ལ་འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་སུ་རང་རང་གི་རྒྱུ་འགག་མོད་ཀྱི།ས་བོན་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགགས༷་ལ༷་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིང༷་ཡང༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེར༷་གྱུར་པ་མིན༷་ཏེ་ས་བོན་འགགས་སུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་མྱུ་གུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིམ་པར་སྣང་བ་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར། ལམ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་དཔྱད་པའི་སྐབས་འདིར་ཡང་དཔེ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་སེམས་ཐོག་མར་བསྐྱེད་པའམ་དང༷་པོའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ༷། སེམས་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགག༷ས་ལ༷་དེའི་བརྒྱུད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེ༷་ལྟ་བུ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་བསླུ་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སེམས་སྔ་ཕྱིའི་རྒྱུ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་མི་བསླུ་བར་ཡོད་དོ། །
[1-281] translation already produced for this document:
The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. "Likewise" here on the occasion of investigating the fruit of the path, "even" the initially generated mind, or the "first" "mind", "is" the "cause" of "awakening", and it is "not" the case that "that" mind "ceases" "and" its indirect fruit, "awakening", is "nonexistent"; by way of infallible cause and effect, the attainment of the fruit, awakening, from the causes, the prior and subsequent minds of the stages of the path, exists infallibly.

heading: **ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second is how to practice that profound nature. In this, there are two: the actual practice, and explaining its qualities.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

དང་པོ། འབྲུ་མར་སྙིང་པོ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ན་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་ནི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཡིན་ལ་དེ་བསག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་དེས་སྒྲིབ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཐོབ་སྟེ་སེམས་སྔ་མ་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་སྒྲིབ་པ་མི་སྤོང་ལ། སྔ་མ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པའི་ཕྱི་མ་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་མི་སྤོང་ཞིང་དེ་གཉིས་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་བསགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། ཐོག་མར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་གྲགས་པའི་དཔེར་བྱ་ན། ཇི་ལྟར་འབྲུ༷་ལ་སོགས་པའི་མར༷་གྱི་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་སྟེ་ཞུན་མར་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དང་མར་མེའི་མེ་ལྕེ་འབར༷་བ༷་གཉིས་ཕྲ༷ད་པ༷་ན། མེ་ལྕེ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིས༷་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང་པོ་དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་དེ༷་མི༷་ཚིག༷་པ་དང་། མར་ཁུ་དང་མེ༷་ལྕེ༷་ཕྲ༷ད་པ༷་ཐ༷་མ༷་ཁོ་ནས་ཀྱང་མར་གྱི་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ༷་མེ༷་ལྕེ༷་ཐ༷་མ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང་སྙིང༷་པོ༷་དེ་ཚིག༷་པ་མིན༷་མོད་ཀྱི། མེ་ལྕེ་སྐད་ཅིག་དང་པོ་ནས་ཐ་མའི་བར་གྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་གི་རྒྱུན་རྫོགས་པ་ན་འབྲུ་མར་གྱི་སྙིང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེས་ཚིག་པར་བྱས་ནས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་དཔེར་བྱས་ནས་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
[1-277] translation already produced for this document:
The first. "The core of grains or oil" and so forth is one verse. Thus, if one says: "Even in terms of conventional designations, the mind that attains awakening is momentary and cannot be accumulated; therefore, how does that mind attain awakening, free from obscurations? Because the former mind alone does not abandon obscurations, and the latter alone, not depending on the former, does not abandon them either, and the two are not accumulated together." First, to use an example well known in the world: just as when the two, the "core" "of" oil such as "grains" and so forth, which is liquid oil, and the "flame" of a lamp "burning" "meet", it is "not" "burned" up completely "by" that "first" momentary flame alone, "nor" is "it" "burned" "without" "that" first one; and the "core" of the oil is "not" "burned" by the "last" "meeting" of the liquid oil and the "flame" alone, "nor" is the "core" "burned" "without" the "last" "flame"; nevertheless, when the continuum of moments from the first momentary flame to the last is complete, the core of the oil or butter is all burned by the fire and completely exhausted—this exists. One should understand this by using it as an example.

[1-278] source:
གཉིས་པ་དང་པོའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་མ་ཐག་པ་དང༷་པོའི༷་སེམ༷ས་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཙམ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས༷་སྤང་བྱ་མཐའ་དག་དང་བྲལ་བའི་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མཆོག༷་ལ་རེག༷་པ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ལ༷། དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ༷་ལ༷་རེག༷་པར༷་ནུས༷་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཞིང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་ཁ་མ་རྒྱུན་གྱི་ཐ༷་མའི༷་སེམ༷ས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་གཅིག་པུ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས༷་ཀྱང་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཆེན་པོ་དྲི་མ་མཐའ་དག་ཞི༷་བ༷་ཐོབ༷་པ་མིན༷་ལ༷། དེ༷་མེ༷ད་པར༷་ཡང༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ༷་ཐོབ༷་པར་ནུས༷་པ༷་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་མོད་ཀྱི་སྔ་མ་སྔ་མ་ལས་ཕྱི་མ་ཕྱི་མ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་གྱིས་མཐར་སྤང་བྱ་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པ་ནི་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བསྙོན་དུ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ༷། །
[1-278] translation already produced for this document:
The second. "Even the first mind" and so forth is one verse. Like the example just explained, the "supreme" "awakening" free from all that is to be abandoned is "not" "touched" "by" the "first" "mind" just after generation alone; "nor" "can" "that" awakening be "touched" "without" "it"; and the great "awakening" where all stains are "pacified" is "not" "attained" "by" the "last" "mind" of the continuum on the verge of attaining awakening alone either, "nor" "can" "that" awakening be "attained" "without" "it"; nevertheless, the attainment of the great awakening where all that is to be abandoned has finally been abandoned by the continuum of mind where each subsequent moment has become more distinguished than the preceding is the nature of dependent origination, undeniable.

The first. In this, there are two: the way it is not unjustified, and explaining how it is definitely justified by way of dependent origination.

[1-281] source:
དང་པོ། ས་བོན་ལས་ནི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། གང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སེམས་དང་པོ་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་དུ་སྡོད་ན་རྟག་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། མི་སྡོད་པར་འགག་ན་སྐད་ཅིག་མའི་སེམས་དེ་སྙེད་པ་རེ་རེ་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འབྱུང་བ་མེད་པས་བསྐལ་པ་དུ་མར་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་འབྱུང་བ་འདི་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མི་འཐད་དོ་ཞེས་རྒོལ་བ་ལ་ལན་བསྟན་པ་ནི། འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་རྒྱུ་ཡི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་རྣམས་སྔོན་དུ་སོང་བ་ན་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་བཤོལ་དུ་མེད་པ་ནི་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ས༷་བོན༷་ལ༷ས་ནི༷་མྱུ༷་གུ༷་དང་དེ་ལས་སྡོང་བུ་མེ༷་ཏོག༷་དང་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་རྣམ༷ས་རིམ་པར་འབྱུང༷་བ་ཡོད་ལ་འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་སུ་རང་རང་གི་རྒྱུ་འགག་མོད་ཀྱི།ས་བོན་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགགས༷་ལ༷་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིང༷་ཡང༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེར༷་གྱུར་པ་མིན༷་ཏེ་ས་བོན་འགགས་སུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་མྱུ་གུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིམ་པར་སྣང་བ་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར། ལམ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་དཔྱད་པའི་སྐབས་འདིར་ཡང་དཔེ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་སེམས་ཐོག་མར་བསྐྱེད་པའམ་དང༷་པོའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ༷། སེམས་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགག༷ས་ལ༷་དེའི་བརྒྱུད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེ༷་ལྟ་བུ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་བསླུ་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སེམས་སྔ་ཕྱིའི་རྒྱུ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་མི་བསླུ་བར་ཡོད་དོ། །
[1-281] translation already produced for this document:
The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The first. "Empty, signless" and so forth is one verse. Thus, because all dharmas are in their own essence "empty", the meaning of thoroughly pacifying all views that apprehend them; and because the basis or cause of such apprehension is "signless", the meaning of thoroughly abandoning all conceptions and discernments; and because of that, because one has no clinging to it or is "wishless" for a fruit, the meaning of being free from prayers for all three realms—thus, "practicing" the profound "dharma" of realizing the three doors of liberation, the meaning of the equality of existence and peace; and by the power of that, "not" "touching" "nirvana", which is the one-sided peace, and "not" "practicing" the "signs" of clinging to entities in existence, is "for" "example", when a "skilled" "ferryman" "goes" to the far shore and near shore of the ocean, he "does" "not" "abide" at the "two" "extremes" of far and near, "nor" "is" he "stationed" "in" the "ocean". Moreover, on this occasion of the perfection of wisdom, whatever synonyms are taught, such as the three liberations, non-arising, suchness, and reality, all accord in a single meaning: whatever is emptiness is also signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth, so although those various synonyms differ in their isolates, they should be understood as one in the meaning of the dharmadhātu to be realized, like the single taste of honey.

The second is the justification for the completion of qualities. "By drops of water" and so forth is one verse. If one asks: "Since entities are momentary and cannot be accumulated, even if one habituates for countless eons, it is impossible for them to gather together and increase, so how does one attain the fruit of awakening where all qualities are complete and perfected?" Although all entities are momentary, because each subsequent mind becomes distinguished in qualities in dependence upon each preceding mind, there is ultimately a complete perfection of qualities. Thus, when a "pot" is filled "by" accumulating "drops" "of" "water" from one to many, just "as" accumulating "gradually", "little" by "little", from the "first" drop to the "last", finally "fills" "that" pot "completely", thus, the attainment of buddhahood in dependence on completing the number of mind-generations gradually over the ten grounds and five paths is "likewise" according to that example: "even" the "first" "mind" generated during the stage of earnest conduct is the "cause" of "supreme" "awakening", and although qualities are not completely perfected by that alone, one "will" attain "buddhahood" through the door of "perfecting" "white" "qualities" "gradually" higher and higher, just as a pot is not filled completely by one drop of water but is filled by many. By means of filling with many instead of filling with one, it becomes the example for attaining buddhahood through the completion of many moments of mind generation; and although the entity of water is momentary, just as the pot is filled by the mutual gathering of the continuum of drops, one should understand that each subsequent moment becoming distinguished from the preceding by the continuum of momentary minds is also in that manner.

The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear.
