The second is the justification for the completion of qualities. "By drops of water" and so forth is one verse. If one asks: "Since entities are momentary and cannot be accumulated, even if one habituates for countless eons, it is impossible for them to gather together and increase, so how does one attain the fruit of awakening where all qualities are complete and perfected?" Although all entities are momentary, because each subsequent mind becomes distinguished in qualities in dependence upon each preceding mind, there is ultimately a complete perfection of qualities. Thus, when a "pot" is filled "by" accumulating "drops" "of" "water" from one to many, just "as" accumulating "gradually", "little" by "little", from the "first" drop to the "last", finally "fills" "that" pot "completely", thus, the attainment of buddhahood in dependence on completing the number of mind-generations gradually over the ten grounds and five paths is "likewise" according to that example: "even" the "first" "mind" generated during the stage of earnest conduct is the "cause" of "supreme" "awakening", and although qualities are not completely perfected by that alone, one "will" attain "buddhahood" through the door of "perfecting" "white" "qualities" "gradually" higher and higher, just as a pot is not filled completely by one drop of water but is filled by many. By means of filling with many instead of filling with one, it becomes the example for attaining buddhahood through the completion of many moments of mind generation; and although the entity of water is momentary, just as the pot is filled by the mutual gathering of the continuum of drops, one should understand that each subsequent moment becoming distinguished from the preceding by the continuum of momentary minds is also in that manner.

དང་པོ། ས་བོན་ལས་ནི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། གང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སེམས་དང་པོ་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་དུ་སྡོད་ན་རྟག་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། མི་སྡོད་པར་འགག་ན་སྐད་ཅིག་མའི་སེམས་དེ་སྙེད་པ་རེ་རེ་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འབྱུང་བ་མེད་པས་བསྐལ་པ་དུ་མར་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་འབྱུང་བ་འདི་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མི་འཐད་དོ་ཞེས་རྒོལ་བ་ལ་ལན་བསྟན་པ་ནི། འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་རྒྱུ་ཡི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་རྣམས་སྔོན་དུ་སོང་བ་ན་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་བཤོལ་དུ་མེད་པ་ནི་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ས༷་བོན༷་ལ༷ས་ནི༷་མྱུ༷་གུ༷་དང་དེ་ལས་སྡོང་བུ་མེ༷་ཏོག༷་དང་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་རྣམ༷ས་རིམ་པར་འབྱུང༷་བ་ཡོད་ལ་འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་སུ་རང་རང་གི་རྒྱུ་འགག་མོད་ཀྱི།ས་བོན་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགགས༷་ལ༷་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིང༷་ཡང༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེར༷་གྱུར་པ་མིན༷་ཏེ་ས་བོན་འགགས་སུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་མྱུ་གུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིམ་པར་སྣང་བ་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར། ལམ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་དཔྱད་པའི་སྐབས་འདིར་ཡང་དཔེ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་སེམས་ཐོག་མར་བསྐྱེད་པའམ་དང༷་པོའི༷་སེམ༷ས་ཀྱང༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ༷། སེམས་དེ༷་ཡང༷་འགག༷ས་ལ༷་དེའི་བརྒྱུད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མེ༷ད་པ༷་དེ༷་ལྟ་བུ་མ༷་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་བསླུ་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སེམས་སྔ་ཕྱིའི་རྒྱུ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་མི་བསླུ་བར་ཡོད་དོ། །

The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. "Likewise" here on the occasion of investigating the fruit of the path, "even" the initially generated mind, or the "first" "mind", "is" the "cause" of "awakening", and it is "not" the case that "that" mind "ceases" "and" its indirect fruit, "awakening", is "nonexistent"; by way of infallible cause and effect, the attainment of the fruit, awakening, from the causes, the prior and subsequent minds of the stages of the path, exists infallibly.

གཉིས་པ། ས་བོན་རྙེད་ནས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཚུལ་ནི། གང་ཞིག་རང་འབྲས་སྐྱེད་རུང་བའི་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་པའི་ས༷་བོན༷་ཉིད་རྙེད༷་པ་སྟེ་ཡོད་པར་གྱུར་ནས༷་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་འབྲུ༷་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང༷་འབྲས་སཱ༷་ལུ༷་ལ༷་སོ༷གས་པ་འབྱུང༷་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། ས་བོན་དེ༷་ཡི༷་འབྲས༷་བུ༷་ནི་ས་བོན་དེ༷་ལ༷་གདོད་ནས་ཡོ༷ད་པ་མིན༷་ཞིང་འབྱུང་རུང་གི་ཚུལ་དུ་མེ༷ད་པ༷་ཡང་མིན༷་ཏེ་གང་སྔ་ནས་ཡོད་པ་ལ་རྒྱུ་མི་དགོས་ཤིང་འབྱུང་རུང་གི་ཚུལ་དུ་མེད་ན་ནི་རྒྱུ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་དེ་ཡི་རང་བཞིན་ལ་དཔྱད་ན་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བ་ཡིན་ན་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚུལ་དུ་སྣང་བ་བསླུ་མེད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་འབྱུང་བ་ནི་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཡི་ཚུལ་དུ་རྒྱལ༷་བ༷་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱི༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་འདི༷་ཡང༷་ནི་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་དབང་གིས་འབྱུང༷་བར༷་འགྱུར༷་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་དངོས༷་པོའི༷་རང༷་བཞིན༷་དང་བྲལ༷་བ་ཡིན་པས༷་སྒྱུ༷་མ༷་ལྟ་བུར་འབྱུང༷་བར༷་འགྱུར་བ་ཉིད་དུ་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །

The second. "Having found a seed" and so forth is one verse. Thus, the way of dependent origination is as follows. "Having found", that is, having come to possess, a "seed" itself that is endowed with the collection suitable to generate its own fruit, its fruit, various "grains" "and" "rice" and "so forth", "will arise", and "the" "fruit" "of" "that" seed is "not" "existent" in "that" seed from the beginning, nor is it "nonexistent" in the manner of being suitable to arise, because whatever exists previously does not need a cause, and if it were nonexistent in the manner of being suitable to arise, the meaning of "cause" would become nonexistent. If it is like that, when its nature is investigated, although it is free from the nature of an entity such as existent or nonexistent, arising infallibly as an appearance in the manner of an illusion and so forth is the way of the dharma of dependent origination. The second is the justification for the completion of qualities. "By drops of water" and so forth is one verse. If one asks: "Since entities are momentary and cannot be accumulated, even if one habituates for countless eons, it is impossible for them to gather together and increase, so how does one attain the fruit of awakening where all qualities are complete and perfected?" Although all entities are momentary, because each subsequent mind becomes distinguished in qualities in dependence upon each preceding mind, there is ultimately a complete perfection of qualities. Thus, when a "pot" is filled "by" accumulating "drops" "of" "water" from one to many, just "as" accumulating "gradually", "little" by "little", from the "first" drop to the "last", finally "fills" "that" pot "completely", thus, the attainment of buddhahood in dependence on completing the number of mind-generations gradually over the ten grounds and five paths is "likewise" according to that example: "even" the "first" "mind" generated during the stage of earnest conduct is the "cause" of "supreme" "awakening", and although qualities are not completely perfected by that alone, one "will" attain "buddhahood" through the door of "perfecting" "white" "qualities" "gradually" higher and higher, just as a pot is not filled completely by one drop of water but is filled by many. By means of filling with many instead of filling with one, it becomes the example for attaining buddhahood through the completion of many moments of mind generation; and although the entity of water is momentary, just as the pot is filled by the mutual gathering of the continuum of drops, one should understand that each subsequent moment becoming distinguished from the preceding by the continuum of momentary minds is also in that manner.

The first. "From a seed" and so forth is one verse. If one objects: "If the first mind that attains awakening abides until the fruit is attained, it would be permanent. If it ceases without abiding, then since awakening does not arise from each of those many momentary minds individually, this arising of the qualities of awakening accomplished over many eons is unjustified conventionally"—the answer to this is taught. Although all conditioned things are momentary, when the moments of the cause have preceded, their fruit is inevitable; this is the nature of dependent origination. Thus in the world, a "sprout" and from that a stalk, a "flower", "and" "fruits" "arise" sequentially "from" a "seed", and at the time of the fruit their respective causes cease; nevertheless, it is "not" the case that "that" seed "ceases" "and" its fruit, the "tree", "is" "nonexistent" either—rather, even though the seed has ceased, the fruits like the sprout and so forth sequentially appear. The second is the justification for the completion of qualities. "By drops of water" and so forth is one verse. If one asks: "Since entities are momentary and cannot be accumulated, even if one habituates for countless eons, it is impossible for them to gather together and increase, so how does one attain the fruit of awakening where all qualities are complete and perfected?" Although all entities are momentary, because each subsequent mind becomes distinguished in qualities in dependence upon each preceding mind, there is ultimately a complete perfection of qualities. Thus, when a "pot" is filled "by" accumulating "drops" "of" "water" from one to many, just "as" accumulating "gradually", "little" by "little", from the "first" drop to the "last", finally "fills" "that" pot "completely", thus, the attainment of buddhahood in dependence on completing the number of mind-generations gradually over the ten grounds and five paths is "likewise" according to that example: "even" the "first" "mind" generated during the stage of earnest conduct is the "cause" of "supreme" "awakening", and although qualities are not completely perfected by that alone, one "will" attain "buddhahood" through the door of "perfecting" "white" "qualities" "gradually" higher and higher, just as a pot is not filled completely by one drop of water but is filled by many. By means of filling with many instead of filling with one, it becomes the example for attaining buddhahood through the completion of many moments of mind generation; and although the entity of water is momentary, just as the pot is filled by the mutual gathering of the continuum of drops, one should understand that each subsequent moment becoming distinguished from the preceding by the continuum of momentary minds is also in that manner.

translation: The first. "Bodhisattvas" and so forth is one verse. The "bodhisattvas" in all respects "practice" and "abide" "in" the mother of the "Victorious Ones", the perfection of "wisdom". How is that? By the power of the subject, wisdom, having "known" "all" "these" dharmas, the "aggregates" and so forth, to be "empty" "and" "without" "arising" "from" the "beginning", they rest in equipoise on the meaning of dharmatā in a non-dual manner; yet just as during the occasion of "not" being "in" "equipoise", great "compassion" "engages" "the" various and measureless "realms" "of" "sentient" "beings", they do not abandon the welfare of sentient beings by abiding solely in the space of peace through resting in equipoise, because they have attained the exceptional profound yoga of the unity of wisdom and compassion. "Also" "in" "that" "meantime" of engaging in the various welfares of sentient beings, they "do" "not" "completely" "degenerate" "from" the non-abiding abiding of the "dharma" "of" the "Buddhas", the perfection of wisdom, because they have attained the wisdom of skillful means in which wisdom and compassion are non-dual. Here, "not in equipoise" is also commented upon as meaning that compassion engages the confused realms of sentient beings who are not in equipoise on the profound meaning of dharmatā; and that compassion engages the realms of sentient beings during the occasion when the bodhisattvas themselves are not in equipoise; and that during those occasions like abiding in the middle or between, which is the unity of wisdom and compassion, they do not completely degenerate from the dharmas of the Buddha, the powers and so forth, so because they possess such skillful means they do not actualize mere peace. In any case, it teaches the essence of skillful means, the unity of wisdom and compassion.

source: གཉིས་པ་ལ་དཔེ་བརྒྱད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བསྟན་ཏེ། སྒྱུ་མའི་དཔེས་སེམས་ཅན་མི་འདོར་བ། སྣོད་ཀྱི་དཔེས་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཤུགས་རྫོགས་པ། བྱ་འཕུར་བའི་དཔེས་རྟེན་མེད་ཀྱང་མི་ལྟུང་བ། མདའ་འཕང་པའི་དཔེས་མ་རྫོགས་པར་སྡོད་པ། རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་དཔེས་སྡོད་ཀྱང་གཞན་དོན་དུ་མི་སྐྱོ་བ། གདུགས་འཛིན་པའི་དཔེས་མཐར་མི་ལྟུང་བ། དེད་དཔོན་གྱི་དཔེས་རང་གཞན་གྱི་ཕན་བདེ་བསྒྲུབ་པ། ཚོང་པའི་དཔེས་ལམ་ལ་མཁས་པ་དང་བརྒྱད་ལས།
translation: The second is taught by means of eight examples: from among the eight—not abandoning sentient beings by the example of an illusion, perfecting the force of prayers by the example of a vessel, not falling despite having no support by the example of a flying bird, remaining until completion by the example of shooting an arrow, not tiring of the welfare of others even while remaining by the example of magical emanations, not falling to an extreme by the example of holding a parasol, accomplishing the benefit and happiness of oneself and others by the example of a captain, and being skilled in the path by the example of a merchant—

Thus, because all dharmas are in their own essence "empty", the meaning of thoroughly pacifying all views that apprehend them; and because the basis or cause of such apprehension is "signless", the meaning of thoroughly abandoning all conceptions and discernments; and because of that, because one has no clinging to it or is "wishless" for a fruit, the meaning of being free from prayers for all three realms—thus, "practicing" the profound "dharma" of realizing the three doors of liberation, the meaning of the equality of existence and peace; and by the power of that, "not" "touching" "nirvana", which is the one-sided peace, and "not" "practicing" the "signs" of clinging to entities in existence, is "for" "example", when a "skilled" "ferryman" "goes" to the far shore and near shore of the ocean, he "does" "not" "abide" at the "two" "extremes" of far and near, "nor" "is" he "stationed" "in" the "ocean". Moreover, on this occasion of the perfection of wisdom, whatever synonyms are taught, such as the three liberations, non-arising, suchness, and reality, all accord in a single meaning: whatever is emptiness is also signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth, so although those various synonyms differ in their isolates, they should be understood as one in the meaning of the dharmadhātu to be realized, like the single taste of honey.

translation: When encountering that host of enemies, "that" "person", being undaunted himself, is "brave" "and" manifestly "emanated" "many" "courageous" "persons" capable of attacking the opponent, ensuring that no harm whatsoever arose from the enemies and so forth, "went" "happily" to whatever destination he desired out there, "and" "like" that "again" "returned" happily "to" his "home"; just as in "that" example, here too during the occasion of the bodhisattva accomplishing the path, "at" "that" "time" of practicing for the welfare of wanderers, "also" the "bodhisattva" who is "skilled" in "means" "generates" "great" "compassion" "in" "all" the "realms" of "sentient" "beings", "and" "having" "completely" "passed" "beyond" the obstacles to the Mahāyāna path—the "four" "māras" such as the Devaputra māra, "and" "also" "from" the "two" "levels" of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, "abiding" "in" the "supreme" "samādhi" endowed with the three gateways to liberation, "does" "not" "touch" "enlightenment" by way of actualizing only the space of peace, the perfect limit. Although one might think, "Since the perfect limit in general is solely devoid of all fabrications, is it possible that great bodhisattvas on the pure bhūmis, whose non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise has fully ripened and merged with that in a single taste, might pass into nirvāṇa prematurely solely in that space of peace?", that is not possible; because they are completely embraced by skillful means, they do not actualize the perfect limit until the dharmas of the Buddha are perfected; and as for what is said in other sūtras about preventing the extreme of peace by way of the Buddhas rousing them from peace through exhortation and so forth, it is not because the essence of the dharmadhātu, the perfect limit, has some basis for falling into the extreme of peace. If it did, it would not be the perfection of wisdom, the basis that by its very nature does not abide in existence or peace. Therefore, realizing it would not even be fit to be the knowledge of the basis that is near to the motherly result, and so forth, and thus, missing the vital point of the Mahāyāna, the perfection of wisdom would become a path common to the three vehicles, but would not be suitable as the uncommon path of the Mahāyāna. Well then, what is it? Because the dharmadhātu, the perfect limit, is in its own essence the meaning of the ultimate natural state, the equality wherein the two truths are indivisible, it does not abide in existence or peace; and since actualizing it just as it is is Buddhahood itself, it is impossible to actualize it on the path of training because the causes for actualizing it are incomplete. Well then, one might think, "Since there is no need for doubt about that, why do they speak of skillful means for not actualizing it prematurely?" During the path of training, because the parts of means and wisdom are present in greater or lesser degrees, it is from the perspective of grasping the perfect limit in terms of its lack of referent and thinking, "If by some chance one were to cling solely to that, it would become one-sided peace," and thereby teaching skillful means to clear away the grasping at extremes, in order to understand that the perfect dharmadhātu, the ultimate emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, is a profound dharma into which even those on the pure bhūmis must enter further; it is the nature of things that on the eighth bhūmi, by the power of one's inner skillful means, and as an outer condition for one abiding in that, the Buddhas also exhort them, saying, "Son of noble family, you have not attained my dharmas, the powers and so forth, so make effort! Generate compassion for the immeasurable realms of sentient beings!"; and because that eighth-bhūmi bodhisattva, though having attained the effortless yoga of abiding in the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, has a predominance of the samādhi of the aspect of wisdom abiding in the space of peace, they still have not attained equality with the Buddhas, whose domain is to rest in equipoise on the ultimate where means and wisdom are subsumed into a single unity without unevenness, the fully pure nature of the dharmadhātu endowed with all supreme aspects; so the meaning is that they must enter the path higher and higher again. The meaning is not in any way that there could by some chance be someone on the pure bhūmis who would pass into nirvāṇa prematurely. Even from the first bhūmi, because they have manifestly seen the dharmatā in which the two truths are indivisible, they are certain to be in the Buddha family, yet just as on the seven impure bhūmis, because they have not attained non-conceptual wisdom in the same way as on the pure bhūmis, there is a predominance of abiding on the side of skillful means. Regarding that, if one asks, "Do not the sūtras say that if by some chance they were not exhorted by the Buddhas, they would undoubtedly pass into nirvāṇa?" That is indeed so; but that is stated as an example of hypothetical extreme reasoning in order to understand that the samādhi of the eighth bhūmi is exceptionally peaceful. It is entirely impossible for the Buddhas not to exhort them, for it is the nature of things that by the power of their inner wisdom of skillful means, the outer condition of exhortation acts in that way to accomplish the perfect gate; and not only that, but since this is so even from when they are born into the Mahāyāna family and attain the first bhūmi of non-returning, what need is there to speak of this? Therefore, if one passes into nirvāṇa prematurely without attaining the ultimate result, the great non-abiding nirvāṇa of Buddhahood itself, it could only be the one-sided nirvāṇa of peace; and while the skillful means for not passing into that is nothing other than the perfection of wisdom itself—the non-duality of emptiness and compassion which is the subject for which the two truths are indivisible—it is a very crucial point to understand that what is taught here is an occasion of practice on the pure bhūmis, an uncommon way of engaging in such skillful means. I have explained this by analyzing slightly a highly important point of doubt.

heading: **སྣོད་ཀྱི་དཔེས་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཤུགས་རྫོགས་པ།**
translation: Second, two verses starting with "wind resting on space": When the world forms and remains, first the maṇḍala of wind rests on space and forms. On that wind rests a mass of water, and on that water rests this great earth. On that earth rest the beings, such as the four continents, that remain on the earth. Such is the cause or basis for sentient beings to experience the karma they have accumulated in common. Even though the elements thus come to rest on one another, ultimately, on what does space rest and remain? Think about this meaning, and you will understand how it does not rest on anything.

translation: Likewise, the bodhisattva remains in emptiness, which is like space. Moreover, knowing the conventions of sentient beings and the ultimate nature of those beings, through objectless great compassion they make immeasurable aspirations for their sake. Supported by this—that is, based on these aspirations—they display various kinds of activities for the benefit and happiness of all realms of sentient beings. The meaning is that they accumulate the provisions until the actions fulfilling their aspirations are entirely perfected.

Remaining in the signless meaning, they experience peace, the pacification of the concepts of saṃsāra, and supreme peace, the pacification of the concepts of nirvāṇa. Just as a bird flying in the sky does not have another place to rest on, and in that space it does not abide anywhere, yet it does not fall to the ground, similarly, the bodhisattva who engages in the doors of liberation does not touch nirvāṇa as an extreme through skillful means, and does not engage in the signs of existence through wisdom. Thus, they do not abide in any phenomenon and do not fall into any extreme.

Fourth, two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery": For example, a person well trained in archery shoots an arrow into the sky along with a flat piece of wood. Then, with other arrows following that one, by continuously attaching them one behind the other, linking them together, that previous arrow finds no opportunity to fall to the ground and is pushed upward. If those people wish to put aside that effort and do not shoot, those arrows will fall to the ground. Like that example, those who engage in the supreme perfection of wisdom during the phase of the path, engaging through objectless wisdom and means such as compassion and full dedication, as well as the powers of faith and so forth, and miraculous abilities such as displaying whatever body is desired—as long as their roots of virtue, which perfectly complete, ripen, and purify, have not been perfected, they will not attain that supreme emptiness, the undefiled expanse, in the meantime. The meaning is that they accumulate the provisions until the actions fulfilling their aspirations are entirely perfected.

heading: **གདུགས་འཛིན་པའི་དཔེས་མཐར་མི་ལྟུང་བ།**
translation: Sixth, two verses starting with "For example, some people": For example, some people stand at the edge of a great abyss and, holding two parasols in their two hands, jump into space and cast their bodies into the great abyss; yet, through the power of the wind lifting the held parasols, they do not immediately fall to the bottom of the abyss, but go slowly for as long as that distance is. Likewise, if a bodhisattva who is wise in suchness and whose mind abides in compassion fully holds the parasols of the two, means and wisdom: by thus holding the parasol of wisdom, they realize phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, and by holding the parasol of means, they do not touch the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa, and they also see all phenomena whatsoever.

Third, two verses starting with "Whenever": Whenever training on the path of the Great Vehicle, a bodhisattva thus becomes wise regarding the ultimate truth and illuminates by dispelling the darkness of others' ignorance. When engaging in this supreme samādhi of peace, pacifying elaborations and taking emptiness as its object, at that time during their training on the path, they do not meditate at all on signs to be apprehended. Remaining in the signless meaning, they experience peace, the pacification of the concepts of saṃsāra, and supreme peace, the pacification of the concepts of nirvāṇa. Just as a bird flying in the sky does not have another place to rest on, and in that space it does not abide anywhere, yet it does not fall to the ground, similarly, the bodhisattva who engages in the doors of liberation does not touch nirvāṇa as an extreme through skillful means, and does not engage in the signs of existence through wisdom. Thus, they do not abide in any phenomenon and do not fall into any extreme.

Fourth, two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery": For example, a person well trained in archery shoots an arrow into the sky along with a flat piece of wood. Then, with other arrows following that one, by continuously attaching them one behind the other, linking them together, that previous arrow finds no opportunity to fall to the ground and is pushed upward. If those people wish to put aside that effort and do not shoot, those arrows will fall to the ground. Like that example, those who engage in the supreme perfection of wisdom during the phase of the path, engaging through objectless wisdom and means such as compassion and full dedication, as well as the powers of faith and so forth, and miraculous abilities such as displaying whatever body is desired—as long as their roots of virtue, which perfectly complete, ripen, and purify, have not been perfected, they will not attain that supreme emptiness, the undefiled expanse, in the meantime. The meaning is that they accumulate the provisions until the actions fulfilling their aspirations are entirely perfected.

heading: **དེད་དཔོན་གྱི་དཔེས་རང་གཞན་གྱི་ཕན་བདེ་བསྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? Like that example, when a bodhisattva goes to the island of precious things of the samādhi of emptiness and obtains immeasurable qualities such as the joy of dhyāna, the five faculties, and the five powers, they do not delight only themselves by touching nirvāṇa in that way, and they do not place other sentient beings in suffering by failing to benefit them with those qualities, because they accomplish those phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

Second, two verses starting with "wind resting on space": When the world forms and remains, first the maṇḍala of wind rests on space and forms. On that wind rests a mass of water, and on that water rests this great earth. On that earth rest the beings, such as the four continents, that remain on the earth. Third, two verses starting with "Whenever": Whenever training on the path of the Great Vehicle, a bodhisattva thus becomes wise regarding the ultimate truth and illuminates by dispelling the darkness of others' ignorance. When engaging in this supreme samādhi of peace, pacifying elaborations and taking emptiness as its object, at that time during their training on the path, they do not meditate at all on signs to be apprehended. Remaining in the signless meaning, they experience peace, the pacification of the concepts of saṃsāra, and supreme peace, the pacification of the concepts of nirvāṇa. Just as a bird flying in the sky does not have another place to rest on, and in that space it does not abide anywhere, yet it does not fall to the ground, similarly, the bodhisattva who engages in the doors of liberation does not touch nirvāṇa as an extreme through skillful means, and does not engage in the signs of existence through wisdom. Thus, they do not abide in any phenomenon and do not fall into any extreme.

Fourth, two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery": For example, a person well trained in archery shoots an arrow into the sky along with a flat piece of wood. Then, with other arrows following that one, by continuously attaching them one behind the other, linking them together, that previous arrow finds no opportunity to fall to the ground and is pushed upward. If those people wish to put aside that effort and do not shoot, those arrows will fall to the ground. Like that example, those who engage in the supreme perfection of wisdom during the phase of the path, engaging through objectless wisdom and means such as compassion and full dedication, as well as the powers of faith and so forth, and miraculous abilities such as displaying whatever body is desired—as long as their roots of virtue, which perfectly complete, ripen, and purify, have not been perfected, they will not attain that supreme emptiness, the undefiled expanse, in the meantime. The meaning is that they accumulate the provisions until the actions fulfilling their aspirations are entirely perfected.

heading: **ཚོང་པའི་དཔེས་ལམ་ལ་མཁས་པ།**
translation: Eighth, two verses starting with "For example, seeking": For example, merchants seeking precious things, in order to know the route of the path, go to whatever large cities, towns—that is, medium-sized cities—and small villages there are between their own home and the island of precious things. Yet, knowing that staying there is pointless, they do not remain in those intermediate cities and so forth. Also, knowing that staying on the island of precious things will not benefit their own home, they do not remain even on the island of precious things. As they go along the path, knowing and understanding the route of the path, they do not remain even in their own home, but, being wise in traveling the path, they will go along the path with effort.

Second, two verses starting with "wind resting on space": When the world forms and remains, first the maṇḍala of wind rests on space and forms. On that wind rests a mass of water, and on that water rests this great earth. On that earth rest the beings, such as the four continents, that remain on the earth. Such is the cause or basis for sentient beings to experience the karma they have accumulated in common. Even though the elements thus come to rest on one another, ultimately, on what does space rest and remain? Think about this meaning, and you will understand how it does not rest on anything.

Likewise, the bodhisattva remains in emptiness, which is like space. Moreover, knowing the conventions of sentient beings and the ultimate nature of those beings, through objectless great compassion they make immeasurable aspirations for their sake. Supported by this—that is, based on these aspirations—they display various kinds of activities for the benefit and happiness of all realms of sentient beings. Yet they do not touch nirvāṇa, which is a one-sided result, nor do they remain in emptiness of the path alone.

[1-296] translation already produced for this document:
Third, two verses starting with "Whenever": Whenever training on the path of the Great Vehicle, a bodhisattva thus becomes wise regarding the ultimate truth and illuminates by dispelling the darkness of others' ignorance. When engaging in this supreme samādhi of peace, pacifying elaborations and taking emptiness as its object, at that time during their training on the path, they do not meditate at all on signs to be apprehended. Remaining in the signless meaning, they experience peace, the pacification of the concepts of saṃsāra, and supreme peace, the pacification of the concepts of nirvāṇa. Just as a bird flying in the sky does not have another place to rest on, and in that space it does not abide anywhere, yet it does not fall to the ground, similarly, the bodhisattva who engages in the doors of liberation does not touch nirvāṇa as an extreme through skillful means, and does not engage in the signs of existence through wisdom. Thus, they do not abide in any phenomenon and do not fall into any extreme.

Fourth, two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery": For example, a person well trained in archery shoots an arrow into the sky along with a flat piece of wood. Then, with other arrows following that one, by continuously attaching them one behind the other, linking them together, that previous arrow finds no opportunity to fall to the ground and is pushed upward. If those people wish to put aside that effort and do not shoot, those arrows will fall to the ground. Like that example, those who engage in the supreme perfection of wisdom during the phase of the path, engaging through objectless wisdom and means such as compassion and full dedication, as well as the powers of faith and so forth, and miraculous abilities such as displaying whatever body is desired—as long as their roots of virtue, which perfectly complete, ripen, and purify, have not been perfected, they will not attain that supreme emptiness, the undefiled expanse, in the meantime. The meaning is that they accumulate the provisions until the actions fulfilling their aspirations are entirely perfected.

heading: **ཚོང་པའི་དཔེས་ལམ་ལ་མཁས་པ།**
translation: Likewise, a bodhisattva who seeks the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, while training on the path of means and wisdom, becomes clear in mind about that way: thus, having become wise in the path knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which is like the intermediate cities and so forth—that is, in all the ways of wisdom and the result of full liberation—they themselves do not remain in that inferior path and result; and they do not remain even in the wisdom of a buddha, which is like the island of precious things, in an obsessing manner; and they do not remain even in the unconditioned expanse of nirvāṇa, which is like one's own home, in a savoring manner. Yet, having known the ways of the three paths of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, which is like temporarily traveling on the path, it should be known that it is indeed to accomplish the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings of those respective affinities.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-298] source:
ལྔ་པ། དཔེར་ན་དགེ་སློང་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཏེ། དཔེར༷་ན༷་དགེ༷་སློང༷་རྫུ༷་འཕྲུལ༷་གྱི་སྟོབ༷ས་མཆོག༷་དང་ལྡན༷་པ༷་ཞིག༷་ནམ༷་མཁར༷་གན༷ས་ཏེ་དུས༷་ཅི༷ག་ཆར༷་ཆོ༷་འཕྲུལ༷་སྣ་ཚོགས་རྣམ༷་པར༷་འཕྲུལ༷་པ་འགྲོ༷་བ་དང༷་འཆག༷་པ༷་དང༷་ནི༷་ཉལ༷་བ་དང༷་འདུག༷་པ༷་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་སྟོན༷་ཀྱང་དེ༷་ལ་ནི༷་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་དེས་སེམས་སྐྱོ༷་བ༷་མེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་དེ༷་ཡི་ལུས་ལ༷་དུབ༷་པ༷་མེ༷ད་དོ། །དཔེ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་མཁས༷་པ༷་གང་ཞིག་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྟོང༷་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་གན༷ས་ཤིང༷་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པའི་ཡེ༷་ཤེ༷ས་དང་རྫུ༷་འཕྲུལ༷་གྱི་ཕ༷་རོ༷ལ་ཏུ་སོན༷་པ་ལ༷་ཆོས་གང་ལའང་དམིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་གན༷ས་པ༷་མེ༷ད་ཀྱང་། འགྲོ༷་བ༷་དག༷་ལ༷་རང་རང་དང་འཚམས་པའི་ཕན་བདེའི་བྱ༷་བ༷་སྣ་ཚོགས་རྣམ༷་པ༷་མཐའ༷་ཡས༷་པ་སྟོན༷་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་བསྐལ༷་པ༷་བྱེ༷་བ་ཚད་མེད་པའི་བར༷་དུ་ཡང་ཡིད་སྐྱོ༷་བ༷་མེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་ལུས་དུབ༷་པ༷་གང་ཡང་མེ༷ད་དོ། །
[1-298] translation already produced for this document:
Fifth, two verses starting with "For example, a monk": For example, a monk endowed with the supreme power of miraculous abilities abides in space and simultaneously displays various miracles, showing various actions of walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting; yet he has no mental weariness from those various actions, and his body has no fatigue. Like that example, a wise bodhisattva abides in the meaning of emptiness, which is like space, and, having reached the far shore of wisdom and miraculous abilities through skillful means, does not abide in any phenomenon in an apprehending manner. Yet, they display boundless various actions for the benefit and happiness of beings, appropriate to each of them; and for billions of immeasurable eons, they have no mental weariness and no bodily fatigue whatsoever.

[1-299] source:
དྲུག་པ་དཔེར་ན་མི་འགའ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཏེ། དཔེར༷་ན༷་མི༷་འག༷འ་ཞིག་གཡང༷་ས༷་ཆེན༷་པོའི༷་ཁར་འདུག༷་པར་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་ལག༷་པ༷་གཉི༷ས་ཀས༷་གདུགས༷་གཉི༷ས་འཛིན༷་ཅིང༷་ནམ༷་མཁའ༷་ལ༷་མཆོང༷ས་པར༷་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་གཡང༷་ས༷་ཆེན༷་པོར༷་ལུས༷་བོར༷་ན༷་གདུགས་ཐོགས་པ་དེ་རླུང་གིས་བཏེགས་པའི་མཐུས་དེ་མ་ཐག་ཏུ་གཡང་ས་དེའི་མཐིལ་དུ་ལྟུང༷་བར༷་མི༷་འགྱུར༷་ཏེ་དེའི་བར་ཐག་ཇི༷་སྲི༷ད་པ་དེར༷་ནི༷་དལ་གྱིས་འགྲོ༷་བར༷་འགྱུར༷་བ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས༷་པ༷་དང་ཡིད་སྙིང༷་རྗེར༷་གན༷ས་པ་གང་གིས་ཐབས༷་དང༷་ཤེས༷་རབ༷་གཉི༷ས་ཀྱི༷་གདུག༷ས་ནི༷་ཡོངས༷་སུ་བཟུང༷་སྟེ༷་གནས་ན། འདི་ལྟར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གདུགས་བཟུང་བས་ཆོས༷་རྣམ༷ས་སྟོང༷་པ༷་དང་མཚ༷ན་མ་མེ༷ད་པ་དང་སྨོན༷་པ་མེ༷ད་པར་རྟོགས༷་ཤིང༷་། ཐབས་ཀྱི་གདུགས་བཟུང་བས་ཞི་བ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པའི་མྱ༷་ངན༷་འདས༷་ལ༷་རེག༷་པ༷་མེ༷ད་ལ༷་ཇི་སྙེད་པའི་ཆོས༷་ཀུན་ཀྱང༷་མཐོང༷་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[1-299] translation already produced for this document:
Sixth, two verses starting with "For example, some people": For example, some people stand at the edge of a great abyss and, holding two parasols in their two hands, jump into space and cast their bodies into the great abyss; yet, through the power of the wind lifting the held parasols, they do not immediately fall to the bottom of the abyss, but go slowly for as long as that distance is. Likewise, if a bodhisattva who is wise in suchness and whose mind abides in compassion fully holds the parasols of the two, means and wisdom: by thus holding the parasol of wisdom, they realize phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, and by holding the parasol of means, they do not touch the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa, and they also see all phenomena whatsoever.

[1-300] source:
བདུན་པ་དཔེར་ན་རིན་ཆེན་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཏེ། དཔེར༷་བྱ་ན༷་མི་ཡ་རབས་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཅན་གཉེན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བདེ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རི༷ན་ཆེན༷་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་ཞིག་རིན༷་ཆེན༷་གྱི་གླིང༷་དུ་སོང༷་སྟེ༷། རིན༷་ཆེན༷་མང་པོ་རྙེད༷་ནས༷་ཕྱིར༷་ཡང༷་རང་གི་ཁྱིམ༷་དུ༷་འོང༷་བར་གྱུར༷་པ༷་ན་དེར༷་ནི༷་དེད༷་དཔོན༷་རང་ཉིད་འབའ༷་ཞིག༷་རྙེད་པ་དེས་བདེ༷་བར༷་འཚོ༷་བར་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་གཞན་གཉེན༷་བཤེས༷་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ལ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མི་སྟེར་བར་ཡི༷ད་མི༷་བདེ༷་བར་འཇོག༷་པར་བྱེད་པ༷་མིན༷་པ༷་ལྟར༷་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། གང་ཞེ་ན་དཔེ་དེ༷་བཞིན༷་དུ་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་སྟོང༷་པ་ཉི༷ད་ཀྱི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་རིན༷་པོ༷་ཆེའི༷་གླིང༷་དུ༷་སོང༷་སྟེ༷་བས༷མ་གཏན༷་ཀྱི་དགའ་བ་དང་དབ༷ང་པོ༷་ལྔ་དང་སྟོབ༷ས་ལྔ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཐོབ༷་པ༷་ན། མྱ༷་ངན༷་འདས༷་ལ༷་རེག༷་པ༷་པོ་རང་ཉིད་འབའ༷་ཞིག༷་ཚུལ་དེས་མངོ༷ན་པར་དགའ༷་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང༷་། སེམ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་གཞན་རྣམས་ལ་ཡོན་ཏན་དེས་ཕན་མི་གདགས་པར་སྡུག༷་བསྔལ༷་ཡི༷ད་དུ་འཇོག༷་པར༷་འགྱུར༷་བ་མ་ཡི༷ན་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་དུ་ཆོས་དེ་དག་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[1-300] translation already produced for this document:
Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? Like that example, when a bodhisattva goes to the island of precious things of the samādhi of emptiness and obtains immeasurable qualities such as the joy of dhyāna, the five faculties, and the five powers, they do not delight only themselves by touching nirvāṇa in that way, and they do not place other sentient beings in suffering by failing to benefit them with those qualities, because they accomplish those phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

[1-301] source:
བརྒྱད་པ་དཔེར་ན་དོན་གཉེར་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཏེ། དཔེར༷་ན༷་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་དོན༷་དུ་གཉེར༷་བའི་ཚོང༷་པ༷་དག་ནི་ལམ་གྱི་རྒྱུས༷་ཤེས༷་པར་བྱ༷་བའི༷་ཕྱིར༷། རང་གི་ཁྱིམ་ནས་རིན་པོ་ཆེའི་གླིང་གི་བར༷་གྱི༷་གྲོང༷་ཁྱེར༷་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་དང་། གྲོང༷་རྡལ༷་ཏེ་གྲོང་འབྲིང་པོ་དང་གྲོང༷་ཆུང་ངུ་བ་གང༷་ཡི༷ན་པར༷་འགྲོ༷་ཡང་རང་ཉིད་དེར་འདུག་པ་དོན་མེད་པར་རིག་ནས་བར་གྱི་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེར༷་ཡང༷་མི༷་གན༷ས་ལ། རིན་པོ་ཆེའི་གླིང་དུ་འདུག་ནའང་རང་ཁྱིམ་ལ་མི་ཕན་པར་ཤེས་ནས་རིན༷་ཆེན༷་གླིང༷་དུའང༷་མི༷་གན༷ས་ལ༷། ལམ་དུ་འགྲོ་བཞིན་པ་ལམ་གྱི་རྒྱུས་ཤེས་ཤིང་རིག༷་པ༷་དེ་དག་ཁོ་རང་གི་ཁྱིམ༷་དུའང༷་མི༷་གན༷ས་པར་ལམ༷་བགྲོད་པ་ལ༷་མཁས༷་ཤིང་རྩོལ་བས་ལམ་དུ་འགྲོ་བར༷་འགྱུར༷་རོ།
[1-301] translation already produced for this document:
Eighth, two verses starting with "For example, seeking": For example, merchants seeking precious things, in order to know the route of the path, go to whatever large cities, towns—that is, medium-sized cities—and small villages there are between their own home and the island of precious things. Yet, knowing that staying there is pointless, they do not remain in those intermediate cities and so forth. Also, knowing that staying on the island of precious things will not benefit their own home, they do not remain even on the island of precious things. As they go along the path, knowing and understanding the route of the path, they do not remain even in their own home, but, being wise in traveling the path, they will go along the path with effort.

Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? Like that example, when a bodhisattva goes to the island of precious things of the samādhi of emptiness and obtains immeasurable qualities such as the joy of dhyāna, the five faculties, and the five powers, they do not delight only themselves by touching nirvāṇa in that way, and they do not place other sentient beings in suffering by failing to benefit them with those qualities, because they accomplish those phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? Like that example, when a bodhisattva goes to the island of precious things of the samādhi of emptiness and obtains immeasurable qualities such as the joy of dhyāna, the five faculties, and the five powers, they do not delight only themselves by touching nirvāṇa in that way, and they do not place other sentient beings in suffering by failing to benefit them with those qualities, because they accomplish those phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

Eighth, two verses starting with "For example, seeking": For example, merchants seeking precious things, in order to know the route of the path, go to whatever large cities, towns—that is, medium-sized cities—and small villages there are between their own home and the island of precious things. As they go along the path, knowing and understanding the route of the path, they do not remain even in their own home, but, being wise in traveling the path, they will go along the path with effort.

translation: Second, one verse starting with "For example, a magically emanated": Thus, even though it is impossible to designate them as being either in saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, that bodhisattva does not become entirely unknown and unseen by anyone in all aspects. For example, it is not the case that the body of a magically emanated person does not appear to anyone, and it can also be designated by name; and it should be known that there are also expressions of its manner in the world. And even though designated by name, that emanation does not become another person who is human or non-human. Likewise, the bodhisattva who courses in the door of the three gateways to liberation, even though not abiding in existence or peace, appears in the world and can also be designated by name. Teaching the difference between turning back and not turning back.

Fifth, two verses starting with "For example, a monk": For example, a monk endowed with the supreme power of miraculous abilities abides in space and simultaneously displays various miracles, showing various actions of walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting; yet he has no mental weariness from those various actions, and his body has no fatigue. Like that example, a wise bodhisattva abides in the meaning of emptiness, which is like space, and, having reached the far shore of wisdom and miraculous abilities through skillful means, does not abide in any phenomenon in an apprehending manner. Fifth, two verses starting with "For example, a monk": For example, a monk endowed with the supreme power of miraculous abilities abides in space and simultaneously displays various miracles, showing various actions of walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting; yet he has no mental weariness from those various actions, and his body has no fatigue. Like that example, a wise bodhisattva abides in the meaning of emptiness, which is like space, and, having reached the far shore of wisdom and miraculous abilities through skillful means, does not abide in any phenomenon in an apprehending manner. Yet, they display boundless various actions for the benefit and happiness of beings, appropriate to each of them; and for billions of immeasurable eons, they have no mental weariness and no bodily fatigue whatsoever.

Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? Like that example, when a bodhisattva goes to the island of precious things of the samādhi of emptiness and obtains immeasurable qualities such as the joy of dhyāna, the five faculties, and the five powers, they do not delight only themselves by touching nirvāṇa in that way, and they do not place other sentient beings in suffering by failing to benefit them with those qualities, because they accomplish those phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

[1-301] translation already produced for this document:
Eighth, two verses starting with "For example, seeking": For example, merchants seeking precious things, in order to know the route of the path, go to whatever large cities, towns—that is, medium-sized cities—and small villages there are between their own home and the island of precious things. Yet, knowing that staying there is pointless, they do not remain in those intermediate cities and so forth. Also, knowing that staying on the island of precious things will not benefit their own home, they do not remain even on the island of precious things. As they go along the path, knowing and understanding the route of the path, they do not remain even in their own home, but, being wise in traveling the path, they will go along the path with effort.

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན།**
translation: First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

Seventh, two verses starting with "For example, precious things": For example, a person of noble descent who desires precious things in order to make their relatives and others happy goes to an island of precious things. Having found many precious things, when returning back to their own home, it is to be understood that it is not the case that the merchant lives happily just by what he found himself and causes unhappiness to the host of relatives and friends by not giving them anything at all. Why is that? First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས།**
translation: The signs of irreversibility. First, three verses starting with "The level of an arhat": Through becoming certain in the Mahāyāna path, the union of means and wisdom, "the level of śrāvaka arhats and buddhas of conditions"—which refers to the "wisdom" of pratyekabuddhas—thus the extreme of peace, and "the three realms" of existence, let alone wanting them in actuality, they "do not desire even in dreams"; and "seeing buddhas" surrounded by an ocean of retinues, and seeing them "also teach the Dharma to beings" in dreams and so forth—it should be known that such a one has been "prophesied as irreversible" from unsurpassed awakening into a lower path. Furthermore, the bodhisattva who possesses a compassionate mind, "in dreams," "sees the places of sentient beings in the three lower realms," and "in that instant" "makes aspiration prayers to cut off the continuity of the lower realms," and sees their sufferings being pacified; or again, when asleep or awake, seeing a town blazing with fire, that bodhisattva thinks, "If I am prophesied as irreversible, by this truth and these words of truth, may this fire be pacified!"—through such "blessings of truth," the power of "that mass of fire" being "pacified" is accomplished—it should be known that such a one has been "prophesied as irreversible."

First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས།**
translation: In the "human world," for various "demonic possessions" and "many illnesses," through speaking words of "truth" "possessing a loving heart" that "wants to benefit" and wants to protect them from suffering, and so forth, by the "blessing" of truth, those things "are pacified." "Yet," "without" becoming "conceited" about that ability, thinking "Because I am able to do that, I possess power," and "without developing pride" thinking that they themselves are particularly superior, it should be known that they have attained the "prophecy as irreversible." Thus, showing certainty in the path is the inner warmth; from that, seeing buddhas and so forth in dreams as outer conditions; and whoever is able to display the power of inner qualities manifestly without conceit—that is taught as the sign. The distinction of being deceived by Māra.

First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

First, one verse starting with "If the conduct": If any person fully asks any bodhisattva what the conduct of abiding as a child of the victorious ones is like, and what the faculties—the faith, wisdom, and so forth by which that person has conviction in and considers the profound way—are like; and if that bodhisattva does not fully teach the profound phenomena of emptiness and signlessness to be realized, and does not explain—that is, is unable to explain—the phenomena, signs, and aspects of the stage of not turning back, and so forth, in order to be able to trust that the person is one whose faculties have ripened, it should be known that that one has not been prophesied as irreversible. For example, when illustrated by asking, "How does a bodhisattva who desires to awaken to buddhahood become familiar with emptiness and yet not actualize it?" and when asked what the conduct, faculties, and signs of the irreversible are like, those who have not internalized it themselves cannot explain it. Likewise, the sūtra says: "Those who course in awakening are many, but those who give the answer are few." When someone who has themselves actualized the phenomena of the path of irreversibility answers whatever is asked in a very definitive manner, one can trust them, thinking, "This one is irreversible due to internalizing such profound phenomena"; otherwise, one cannot be certain that they are irreversible.

heading: **མིང་གི་གཞི་ལས་འོང་བའི་བདུད།**
translation: Second, two verses starting with "From the basis of a name": The "māra" of conceit "arises" "also from the basis of a name." What is that? It is like this: the evil māra, in any guise such as a buddha, "approaches" that person and "speaks thus": "Such-and-such is 'your' 'name', and 'that of your parents', and the 'names' of 'your' 'lineage' 'back to the ancestors of seven generations'." Uttering all their names, in accordance with what they had previously thought in their own mind and so forth, he says, "And 'when' 'you' 'become a buddha', 'your name' 'will be' such-and-such!" He clearly states exactly what kind of ascetic practices they are presently abiding in, such as eating almsfood and using a single seat; and that they "possess the vows" of pure discipline; and "what kind" of "yogas" of reflection, meditation, and so forth they will "possess." He "states", "In 'past' times 'too', 'your' 'manner of qualities' such as ascetic practices 'was similar' to 'this' present one." "Hearing" "what" the māra "spoke", that "bodhisattva" who "develops conceit" based on the basis or cause of merely the "names" stating their own qualities and so forth, "should be known" as "having their conceit completely provoked by māra" and having a "small mind".

heading: **ནང་གི་དབེན་པ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: First, one verse starting with "Always in villages": "Always" "abiding in" "villages" such as Videha, "countrysides" such as Campaka, and "towns" such as Pāṭaliputra, they "mature sentient beings" there and "exert themselves in" the path of "awakening"; "apart from" that, "that" bodhisattva "never" "develops" "desire for" the results of "arhats" and "pratyekabuddhas". "This" "is perfectly taught" as the "isolation" "of the sons of the Sugata", the bodhisattvas; for merely being physically isolated does not make the mind isolated from stains, but when the inner mind is isolated from attention to one's own benefit and attention to the lower paths, wherever one abides, one abides in supreme isolation. That is, for example, like the story occurring in the Noble Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra, where the Noble Mañjuśrī formerly promised to observe the summer retreat in the Jeta Grove, but without staying there in the assembly of the saṅgha, he matured sentient beings in the retinue of King Prasenajit's queens.

heading: **ནང་གི་དབེན་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་སྐྱོན།**
translation: First, one verse starting with "Whoever [...] yojanas": Even if "whoever" "abides" "for ten million" "many" "years" "somewhere" that is an uninhabited "mountain valley" "which is" isolated from the comings and goings of people for up to "five hundred" "yojanas", and "full of" venomous "snakes" making it an unbearable place to stay, "that" "bodhisattva" "who does not know" "this" authentic inner "isolation", "having acquired" "superior" "conceit" about themselves, "abides" "mixed with" attention to the lower paths. The reason for this is that isolation means the state of being unmixed. With what is it inappropriate to be mixed? Since it is inappropriate for the mind-stream of a bodhisattva to be mixed with excessive attachment to themselves and attention to the lower paths, the meaning is that if they do not know such isolation, but develop conceit on account of mere physical isolation and "slack off" from working for the benefit of sentient beings, their mind becomes mixed with afflictions, which are disharmonious factors, and thus they do not abide in isolation.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-314] source:
གཉིས་པ་མིང་གི་གཞི་ལས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཏེ། མིང༷་གི༷་གཞི༷་ལ༷ས་ཀྱང་རློམ་པའི་བདུ༷ད་འབྱུང་སྟེ་གང་ཞེ་ན་འདི་ལྟར་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་ནི༷་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆ་བྱད་གང་ཡང་རུང་བས་གང་ཟག་དེའི་གན་དུ་ཉེ༷་བར༷་འོང༷་པར་གྱུར༷་ནས༷། འདི༷་སྐ༷ད་སྨྲས༷་ཏེ༷་འདི༷་ལྟ་བུ་ནི༷་ཁྱོ༷ད་དང༷་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་ཕ༷་མ༷་དང༷་། ཁྱོ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་མི་རབས་བདུན༷་གྱི་མེས༷་པོ་ཚུན་ཆད་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ༷ད་ཀྱི༷་བར་གྱི༷་མིང༷་ཡི༷ན་ནོ་ཞེས་དེ་དག་གི་མིང་ཐམས་ཅད་སྨྲ་ཞིང༷་རང་གི་ཡིད་ལ་སྔོན་ནས་བསམ་པ་སོགས་དང་ཚུལ་མཐུན་པར་གང༷་ཚེ༷་ཁྱོ༷ད་ནི༷་སངས༷་རྒྱས༷་སུ་འགྱུར༷་བའི༷་མིང༷་ནི་འདི༷་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡི༷ན་ནོ། །ད་ལྟ་གང་ཟག་དེ་བསོད་སྙོམས་པ་དང་སྟན་གཅིག་པ་སོགས་སྦྱང༷ས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་གནས་པ་དང་། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དག་པའི་སྡོམ༷་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་སྒོམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རྣལ༷་འབྱོར༷་དང་ལྡན༷་པ༷་ཅི༷་འདྲ༷་བ་འབྱུང༷་བར་འགྱུར༷་བ་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གསལ་པོར་བརྗོད་ལ༷། ཁྱོ༷ད་ཅི་སྔོ༷ན་གྱི་དུས་སུ་ཡང་སྦྱང་ཡོན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན༷་ཏན༷་གྱི་ཚུལ༷་ཡང༷་ད་ལྟའི་འདི༷་དང་འདྲ༷་བར་གྱུར་པའོ་ཞེས༷་བརྗོ༷ད་པར་བྱེད་དོ༷། །དེ༷་སྐ༷ད་སྨྲས་པའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ཚིག་དེ་གང༷་གིས་ཐོས༷་ནས། རང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་སོགས་བརྗོད་པའི་མིང་ཙམ་གྱི་གཞིའམ་རྒྱུ་དེ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེས་རློམ༷་སེམ༷ས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་དེ་ནི༷།བདུ༷ད་ཀྱིས༷་རློམ་སེམས་ཡོངས༷་སུ༷་བསླང༷་ཞིང༷་བློ༷་ཆུང༷་བ་ཡིན་པར་རིག༷་པར༷་བྱའོ༷། །
[1-314] translation already produced for this document:
Second, two verses starting with "From the basis of a name": The "māra" of conceit "arises" "also from the basis of a name." What is that? It is like this: the evil māra, in any guise such as a buddha, "approaches" that person and "speaks thus": "Such-and-such is 'your' 'name', and 'that of your parents', and the 'names' of 'your' 'lineage' 'back to the ancestors of seven generations'." Uttering all their names, in accordance with what they had previously thought in their own mind and so forth, he says, "And 'when' 'you' 'become a buddha', 'your name' 'will be' such-and-such!" He clearly states exactly what kind of ascetic practices they are presently abiding in, such as eating almsfood and using a single seat; and that they "possess the vows" of pure discipline; and "what kind" of "yogas" of reflection, meditation, and so forth they will "possess." He "states", "In 'past' times 'too', 'your' 'manner of qualities' such as ascetic practices 'was similar' to 'this' present one." "Hearing" "what" the māra "spoke", that "bodhisattva" who "develops conceit" based on the basis or cause of merely the "names" stating their own qualities and so forth, "should be known" as "having their conceit completely provoked by māra" and having a "small mind".

[1-315] source:
གསུམ་པ་ལ་མདོར་བསྟན་རྒྱས་བཤད་གཉིས།
[1-315] translation already produced for this document:
Third, there are two: the brief teaching and the detailed explanation.

[1-316] source:
དང་པོ། རབ་ཏུ་དབེན་པའི་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། རང་ཉིད་གཞན་དང་མི་ཕྲད་པར་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་དབེན༷་པའི༷་གྲོང༷་དང༷་གྲོང༷་ཁྱེར༷་ཆེན་པོ་དང་རི༷་ཡི་སུལ༷་དང༷་གྲོང་ལས་ཐག་རིང་བ་དགོན༷་པ༷་དང་མི་མེད་པའི་དབེན༷་པ༷་དང་ནགས༷་ཀྱི་ཁྲོད༷་ལྟ་བུ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་རབ༷་ཏུ༷་བསྟེན༷་པར་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་གནས་མོད་ཀྱི། དེ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་དབེན་པར་གནས་པ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཆོག་ཏུ་བསྔགས་ཤིང་བདག་ནི་དབེན་པར་གནས་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་དབེན་པའི་གཞི་དེས་རློམ་སེམས་སུ་གྱུར་ནས། བདག༷་ལ་བསྟོ༷ད་ཅིང་གཞན༷་དབེན་པར་མི་གནས་པ་ལ༷་སྨོད༷་པའི༷་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་དེ་ནི༷། བདུ༷ད་ཀྱིས༷་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས༷་སུ༷་བསླ༷ད་པའམ་བསྐྱོད་པར་བྱས་ཤིང༷་། དེ་དག་བློ༷་རྒྱ་ཆུང༷་བ་ཉིད་དུ་རིག༷་པར༷་བྱའོ༷། །
[1-316] translation already produced for this document:
First, one verse starting with "Fully isolated": Without encountering others, they "thoroughly rely on" and abide in whatever "fully isolated" "villages", large "cities", "mountain valleys", "wildernesses" far from towns, unpopulated "isolated places", or "forests"; however, thinking "Abiding in isolation is supremely praised by the Tathāgata, and I abide in isolation," they develop conceit about that basis of isolation. "That bodhisattva" who "praises themselves and deprecates others" who do not abide in isolation "should be known" as having their mind-stream "completely corrupted" or agitated "by māra", and having a "small" capacity of "mind".

[1-317] source:
གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནང་གི་དབེན་པ་བསྟན་པ། དབེན་པ་དེ་མ་ཤེས་པའི་སྐྱོན་བཤད་པ་གཉིས།
[1-317] translation already produced for this document:
Second, there are two: teaching inner isolation, and explaining the fault of not knowing that isolation.

[1-318] source:
དང་པོ། རྟག་ཏུ་གྲོང་དང་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། དུས་རྟག༷་ཏུ༷་ལུས་འཕགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟ་བུའི་གྲོང༷་དང༷་ཙམ་པ་ཀ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡུལ༷་འཁོར༷་དང་། པ་ཏྲ་ལི་པུ་ཏྲ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟ་བུའི་གྲོང༷་རྡལ༷་ན་གན༷ས་པར་བྱེ༷ད་ཅིང༷་། དེར་སེམ༷ས་ཅ༷ན་རྣམས་སྨིན༷་པ༷་བྱེ༷ད་པ་དང་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་ཀྱི་ལམ་ལ་བརྩོན༷་པ༷་མ་གཏོགས༷་པ༷ར། བྱང་སེམས་དེ༷་ནི༷་དགྲ༷་བཅོ༷མ་དང་རང༷་རྒྱལ༷་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་འདོ༷ད་པ༷་གཞར༷་ཡང་སྟེ་ནམ་ཡང་མི༷་སྐྱེ་བ་འདི༷་ནི་བདེ༷་བར༷་གཤེ༷གས་པའི་སྲས༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི༷་དབེན༷་པ་ཡང་དག་པར༷་གསུ༷ངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ལུས་དབེན་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་སེམས་དྲི་མས་དབེན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ལ། ནང་གི་སེམས་རང་དོན་ཡིད་བྱེད་དང་དམན་ལམ་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་དབེན་པ་ན་གང་དུ་གནས་ཀྱང་དབེན་པའི་མཆོག་ལ་གནས་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་དག་དཔེར་ན་སྔོན་འཕགས་པ་འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱིས་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་དུ་དབྱར་གནས་པར་དམ་བཅས་ནས་དེར་དགེ་འདུན་གྱི་ཚོགས་སུ་མ་བཞུགས་པར་གསལ་རྒྱལ་གྱི་བཙུན་མོའི་འཁོར་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་སྨིན་པར་བྱས་པའི་ལོ་རྒྱུས་འཕགས་པ་དཀོན་མཆོག་གི་ཟ་མ་ཏོག་ལས་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །
[1-318] translation already produced for this document:
First, one verse starting with "Always in villages": "Always" "abiding in" "villages" such as Videha, "countrysides" such as Campaka, and "towns" such as Pāṭaliputra, they "mature sentient beings" there and "exert themselves in" the path of "awakening"; "apart from" that, "that" bodhisattva "never" "develops" "desire for" the results of "arhats" and "pratyekabuddhas". "This" "is perfectly taught" as the "isolation" "of the sons of the Sugata", the bodhisattvas; for merely being physically isolated does not make the mind isolated from stains, but when the inner mind is isolated from attention to one's own benefit and attention to the lower paths, wherever one abides, one abides in supreme isolation. That is, for example, like the story occurring in the Noble Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra, where the Noble Mañjuśrī formerly promised to observe the summer retreat in the Jeta Grove, but without staying there in the assembly of the saṅgha, he matured sentient beings in the retinue of King Prasenajit's queens.

[1-319] source:
གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནང་གི་དབེན་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་སྐྱོན་དང་། ནང་གི་དབེན་པ་ཅན་ལ་བརྙས་པའི་སྐྱོན་བསྟན་པ་གཉིས།
[1-319] translation already produced for this document:
Second, there are two: the fault of being devoid of inner isolation, and teaching the fault of despising those who possess inner isolation.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: First, one verse starting with "Bodhisattva": "Towards that" "bodhisattva" who is "exerting" themselves "for the benefit" "of wanderers", and "having attained" the four "dhyānas", "and" the five "powers", "and" the five "faculties", and the "samādhis" of the three doors of "liberation", wanders in villages and cities and displays various ways of acting for the purpose of maturing sentient beings, those who do not know their profound intent and conduct and who "despise" them, thinking, "'This one' 'is not' 'practicing' in 'wildernesses' and 'isolated places'"—"that" despiser "is" abiding in the "domain" "of māra", meaning the domain where māra finds an opportunity, "thus" "the Victor" "has taught". This is just as is taught in the Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa Sūtra and elsewhere, in the story of the dharma-preaching monks Viśuddhacāritra and Cāritramati.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

[1-314] translation already produced for this document:
Second, two verses starting with "From the basis of a name": The "māra" of conceit "arises" "also from the basis of a name." What is that? It is like this: the evil māra, in any guise such as a buddha, "approaches" that person and "speaks thus": "Such-and-such is 'your' 'name', and 'that of your parents', and the 'names' of 'your' 'lineage' 'back to the ancestors of seven generations'." Uttering all their names, in accordance with what they had previously thought in their own mind and so forth, he says, "And 'when' 'you' 'become a buddha', 'your name' 'will be' such-and-such!" He clearly states exactly what kind of ascetic practices they are presently abiding in, such as eating almsfood and using a single seat; and that they "possess the vows" of pure discipline; and "what kind" of "yogas" of reflection, meditation, and so forth they will "possess." He "states", "In 'past' times 'too', 'your' 'manner of qualities' such as ascetic practices 'was similar' to 'this' present one." "Hearing" "what" the māra "spoke", that "bodhisattva" who "develops conceit" based on the basis or cause of merely the "names" stating their own qualities and so forth, "should be known" as "having their conceit completely provoked by māra" and having a "small mind".

[1-318] translation already produced for this document:
First, one verse starting with "Always in villages": "Always" "abiding in" "villages" such as Videha, "countrysides" such as Campaka, and "towns" such as Pāṭaliputra, they "mature sentient beings" there and "exert themselves in" the path of "awakening"; "apart from" that, "that" bodhisattva "never" "develops" "desire for" the results of "arhats" and "pratyekabuddhas". "This" "is perfectly taught" as the "isolation" "of the sons of the Sugata", the bodhisattvas; for merely being physically isolated does not make the mind isolated from stains, but when the inner mind is isolated from attention to one's own benefit and attention to the lower paths, wherever one abides, one abides in supreme isolation. translation: The brief teaching. First, one verse starting with "Therefore": Since many activities of māra arise for those seeking the path, "therefore", in order to reverse them, one should rely on outer and inner upholders. What are they like? Who relies on them? By one who "possesses" a "strong" "intent" "seeking" "supreme" "awakening", and who possesses "skill" in the methods to accomplish it. How do they rely? Having "definitely" "destroyed" "conceit" in their own mind-stream, with great respect for another, a spiritual friend, "just as" a "multitude" of "sick people" "rely" on another good "physician" "to" "cure" their own illness, even during the occasion of listening to the dharma, possessing the four recognitions of oneself as a sick person, the dharma preacher as a physician, the dharma as medicine, and earnest practice as curing the illness, they should rely on them "without" "slackening". Upon whom do they rely? A "spiritual" "friend". Here, "virtue" (spiritual) is the dharma of the mahāyāna, and the one who teaches it well is a spiritual friend, because they are able to completely uphold one so as not to deteriorate from the path by authentically teaching the path, making one recognize the interruptions to the path, the activities of māra, and teaching the methods to transcend them. Therefore, they should completely "rely" upon such a one.

translation: First, one verse starting with "Just as the wisdom": In the Noble Eight Thousand-Line Prajñāpāramitā, in response to a question about the defining characteristic of the perfection of wisdom, it states, "The perfection of wisdom is characterized by emptiness," thus teaching the ultimate characteristic without teaching the conventional characteristic; for conventional modes of abiding, such as form being characterized by suitability as form, are not established ultimately, but are merely imputed by the mind and cannot withstand analysis. Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་ཆེན་སྡུད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་དགོངས་དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ལེགས་བཤད། ('Commentary on Precious Qualities: Entering the True Intent of the Buddha''s Mother'), author: འཇུ་མི་ཕམ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

གཉིས་པ་གང་ཞིག་གྲོང་ངམ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང༷་ཞིག༷་ལུས་གྲོང༷་ངམ༷་འོ༷ན་ཏེ༷་དགོན༷་པར༷་གན༷ས་ཀྱང༷་རུང༷་སྟེ། ནང་གི་ཡིད་ཉན་རང་གི་ཐེག༷་པ༷་གཉི༷ས་ཀྱི༷་སེམ༷ས་དང་བྲལ༷་ནས་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་མཆོག༷་གི་ལམ་ལ་ངེས༷་པར་གྱུར་ན༷། ཚུལ་འདི༷་ནི༷་འགྲོ༷་བའི་དོན༷་ལ་ཞུགས༷་པ༷་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམ༷ས་ཀྱི༷་དབེན༷་པ༷་ཡང་དག་པ་སྟེ༷། དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཤེས་ནས་དེ་འདྲའི་དབེན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱང༷་ཆུབ༷་སེམ༷ས་དཔའ༷་འདི་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་གྱིས་དྲོད༷་སྙོམ་པའམ་དྲོད་ཚད་བཟུང་ནས་འདི་ནི་དབེན་པར་མི་གནས་པའོ་སྙམ་པ་སོགས་ཚད་འཛིན་པ་དེ༷་ནི༷་བདག༷་ཉི༷ད་ཐོབ་པ་དང་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལས་ཉ༷མས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། དེས་ན་ང་དང་ང་འདྲ་བ་མ་གཏོགས་པར་གང་ཟག་གིས་གང་ཟག་གི་ཚོད་གཟུང་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞེས་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ནི་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་ལ་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་གཞན་གྱི་འཁྲུལ་པ་བཙལ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞེས་མདོ་རྣམས་སུ་གསུངས་སོ། །༈དེ་སྤང་བའི་ཐབས་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བསྟན་པ།
[1-323] translation already produced for this document:
Second, one verse starting with "Whoever [...] in villages or": Whether "whoever", a bodhisattva, physically "abides" in "villages" "or" "wildernesses", "if" their inner mind is "free from" the "mind" "of the two" śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha "vehicles" and becomes "certain" of the path of "supreme" "awakening", "this" manner "is" the authentic "isolation" "of" bodhisattvas "engaged in" "the benefit of" "wanderers". Not knowing this, if another bodhisattva "evaluates" or takes the measure of "this" "bodhisattva" who possesses such isolation, judging them by thinking, "This one does not abide in isolation" and so forth, "that" evaluator "will" "deteriorate" "themselves" from the qualities they have attained and have not yet attained. Therefore, it is taught in the sūtras, "A person should not take the measure of a person, except for myself and those like me," and "A bodhisattva should examine their own mind-stream, but should not seek out the faults of others." Teaching to exert oneself in the methods to abandon that.
